\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Data Understanding and
Exploration}\label{sec-chapter-data-understanding}

\begin{chapterquote}
You see, but you do not observe. The distinction is clear.

\hfill — Arthur Conan Doyle
\end{chapterquote}

A dataset does not explain itself. Values that appear ordinary may
encode missing information, unusual observations may reflect errors or
meaningful rare cases, and seemingly different features may contain
overlapping information. Before drawing conclusions or building
predictive models, we therefore need to understand what the observations
represent, how the features are defined and measured, whether the
recorded values are plausible, and what patterns and relationships are
present. Developing this understanding is the purpose of the \emph{Data
Understanding and Exploration} stage of the Data Science Workflow.

This stage follows Data Acquisition in the workflow introduced in Figure
\ref{fig-ds_DSW} and provides the empirical foundation for Data
Preparation for Modeling (Chapter \ref{sec-chapter-data-preparation}).
Its purpose is not simply to produce summaries and plots, but to develop
a reliable understanding of the data before analytical decisions are
made. This requires combining knowledge of how the data were defined and
collected with numerical summaries, visualizations, and contextual
reasoning to examine data quality, distributions, relationships, and
potential limitations.

Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is a central component of this stage. It
is primarily investigative rather than confirmatory: it helps us
discover patterns, identify potential problems, compare groups, examine
relationships, and formulate questions for further analysis. These
findings may motivate later data preparation, statistical inference, or
predictive modeling, but they should not be treated as final statistical
or causal conclusions. Formal tools for quantifying uncertainty and
drawing conclusions beyond the observed data are introduced later in
Chapter \ref{sec-chapter-statistics}.

Data understanding and exploration are iterative rather than strictly
linear. An unexpected value may require us to revisit the data source,
an apparent pattern may prompt closer examination of particular
observations or subgroups, and a feature whose meaning is unclear may
require further documentation. An important distinction must therefore
be maintained between identifying and understanding a data issue and
deciding how to address it. This chapter focuses on the former;
decisions about imputation, transformation, encoding, feature
representation, and other procedures used to create a model-ready
dataset belong to the next stage of the workflow, Data Preparation for
Modeling, addressed in Chapter \ref{sec-chapter-data-preparation}.

\subsection*{What This Chapter Covers}\label{what-this-chapter-covers-1}

This chapter develops a systematic approach to data understanding and
exploration. We begin by examining how visualizations can reveal
patterns, support clear data storytelling, and generate questions for
further investigation. We then consider the types and analytical roles
of features, the relationship between their conceptual meaning and
technical representation in R, and the interpretation of numerical
distributions. We also examine how unusual observations and implausible
values can be identified and investigated using graphical, numerical,
and contextual information. Readers who need a review of R fundamentals,
including data frames, indexing, data manipulation, and basic
visualization, can consult Appendix \ref{sec-chapter-r-foundations}.

These principles are applied in a guided case study using the
\texttt{churn} dataset from the \textbf{liver} package. The case study
begins with problem definition, data acquisition, initial inspection,
and assessment of data quality. We then explore categorical and
numerical features and investigate relationships and potential
redundancy among features. Throughout the analysis, numerical summaries,
visualizations, and contextual reasoning are used together to identify
meaningful patterns and limitations while distinguishing exploratory
associations from conclusions that would require formal statistical or
causal evidence.

By the end of the chapter, readers should be able to formulate
appropriate questions for data understanding and exploration, identify
feature types and analytical roles, assess data quality, and investigate
unusual or implausible observations. They should also be able to select
suitable numerical and graphical summaries, compare patterns across
groups, examine relationships and potential redundancy among features,
and communicate exploratory findings clearly without overstating their
implications. Finally, readers should be able to use insights obtained
during exploration to motivate later decisions during Data Preparation
for Modeling.

\section{Seeing Patterns and Data
Storytelling}\label{sec-eda-seeing-patterns}

Data exploration helps reveal patterns, differences, and potential
limitations that are difficult to recognize from raw observations alone.
Visualizations are particularly valuable because they can make
relationships, unusual observations, group differences, and changes over
time visible, while also drawing attention to questions that deserve
closer investigation.

A well-known example is Hans Rosling's TED Talk \emph{New insights on
poverty} (Rosling 2007), in which demographic and economic data are used
to reveal and communicate patterns of global development over time.
Figure \ref{fig-EDA-fig-1} presents a related visualization based on the
\texttt{gapminder} dataset from the \textbf{liver} package. It compares
GDP per capita and life expectancy across countries in 1950 and 2019.
Countries are distinguished by world region, and point size is
proportional to population.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=1\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{2-data-understanding-eda_files/figure-pdf/fig-EDA-fig-1-1.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-EDA-fig-1}GDP per capita and life expectancy across
countries in 1950 (left) and 2019 (right). Countries are grouped by
world region, and point size is proportional to population.}

\end{figure}%

Several patterns are immediately visible. Between 1950 and 2019, both
GDP per capita and life expectancy generally increased, although
substantial differences remained across countries and world regions. The
figure also suggests that countries with higher GDP per capita tend to
have higher life expectancy. At the same time, countries with similar
levels of GDP may differ considerably in life expectancy, indicating
that the relationship is not uniform.

The visualization therefore provides both information and questions. How
strong is the relationship between GDP per capita and life expectancy?
Which countries depart from the overall pattern, and do regional
differences help explain some of this variation? Such questions can
guide further exploration. The observed association is descriptive,
however, and should not be interpreted as evidence that changes in GDP
per capita directly cause changes in life expectancy.

Visual exploration also plays an important role in communicating what we
learn from data. In this context, \emph{data storytelling} means
selecting and organizing relevant graphical and numerical evidence
around a clear question so that the main patterns, their context, and
their limitations can be understood. It does not mean imposing a
predetermined narrative on the data or presenting only the evidence that
supports a preferred conclusion. Effective data storytelling
distinguishes between what is directly observed, how the observed
patterns may be interpreted, and which questions remain unresolved.

Seeing and communicating a pattern is only the beginning. Data
understanding and exploration also require us to investigate what the
pattern represents, whether it is consistent across the dataset, which
observations depart from it, and what additional information may be
needed to interpret it. The next step is therefore to translate visible
patterns into systematic exploratory questions.

\subsection*{From Patterns to
Questions}\label{from-patterns-to-questions}

To move from observation to systematic exploration, we need to translate
visible patterns into questions that can be investigated using the data.
These questions can be organized around three complementary levels:
understanding the dataset as a whole, examining individual features, and
investigating relationships among features. Exploratory data analysis
(EDA) provides numerical and graphical tools for addressing many of
these questions, while contextual information helps determine how the
resulting patterns should be interpreted.

At the dataset level, we ask what each observation represents, how and
when the data were collected, and which population or process the data
describe. We identify the unit of analysis and determine whether the
dataset contains a target feature, predictors, identifiers, derived
measurements, or other features with special analytical roles. These
questions help establish whether the available data are appropriate for
addressing the problem of interest and which limitations should be
considered during exploration.

At the feature level, we examine what each feature means, how it is
represented in R, and which values it can reasonably take. We
investigate its distribution and range, assess the presence of missing
or unspecified information, and look for unusual observations. Relevant
questions include whether a numerical feature is symmetric or skewed,
whether a categorical feature contains rare or placeholder levels, and
whether extreme values represent errors, valid rare cases, or meaningful
subgroups.

At the relationship level, we examine how features vary together. We may
ask whether a numerical feature differs across groups, whether two
numerical features are associated, or whether two categorical features
occur together systematically. We also investigate whether features
contain overlapping information, are mathematically derived from one
another, or reveal patterns only when considered jointly. When a target
feature is available, we may also examine how other features vary across
target groups.

The interpretation of exploratory findings depends on the context in
which the data were defined and collected. A large numerical value may
be unusual but valid in one application and implausible in another.
Similarly, a value such as \texttt{"unknown"} may be stored as an
ordinary categorical level in R while representing missing or
unspecified information. The choice of exploratory tools should
therefore follow from both the question and the feature types involved.
Numerical features may be examined using summary statistics and
distributional plots, categorical features using frequencies and bar
plots, and relationships among features using grouped summaries, scatter
plots, contingency tables, or measures of association. These tools
should be interpreted together with feature definitions, measurement
units, the data-collection process, and relevant domain knowledge.
Systematic exploration therefore depends not only on selecting
appropriate tools, but also on understanding what the data represent and
what questions they can reasonably address.

\section{Feature Types and Data
Representation}\label{sec-eda-feature-types}

Before summarizing, visualizing, or interpreting a dataset, we need to
understand what each feature represents. Feature type determines which
numerical summaries are meaningful, which graphical tools are
appropriate, and how observed patterns should be interpreted. For
example, a numerical feature may be summarized using measures such as
the mean, median, or standard deviation, whereas a categorical feature
is usually described using frequencies or proportions. Treating these
feature types interchangeably can lead to misleading summaries,
inappropriate visualizations, and poor analytical decisions.

It is equally important to consider a feature's analytical role. A
feature may serve as a predictor, a target, an identifier, or a quantity
derived from other features. These roles affect how the feature should
be explored and interpreted. For example, a customer identifier may be
stored as a number, but it represents a label rather than a measurable
quantity and should not be treated as an ordinary numerical feature.

Understanding both feature type and analytical role also provides a
foundation for later Data Preparation for Modeling. Numerical features
may eventually require transformation or scaling, while categorical
features may need encoding or other forms of preparation. Such decisions
should be made only after the meaning, representation, and observed
behavior of the relevant features have been examined carefully.

\subsection*{Numerical and Categorical
Features}\label{numerical-and-categorical-features}

At a high level, most features used in data science can be grouped into
two broad types: numerical and categorical. Each type can be divided
into several common subtypes, as summarized in Figure
\ref{fig-eda-feature-type}.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.65\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{images/ch_eda_feature_type.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-eda-feature-type}Overview of common feature types
used in data analysis, including numerical (continuous and discrete) and
categorical (nominal, ordinal, and binary) features.}

\end{figure}%

Numerical features represent measurable or countable quantities.
Continuous numerical features can take many possible values within a
range, such as income, temperature, transaction amount, or credit limit.
Discrete numerical features take countable values, often integers, such
as the number of purchases, customer-service contacts, website visits,
or product defects. The distinction is not always absolute because it
may depend on how a quantity is recorded. For example, age may be
recorded in whole years but still represents an underlying quantitative
characteristic.

Categorical features describe membership in groups rather than numerical
magnitude. Nominal features represent categories without an inherent
order, such as region, product type, or marital status. Ordinal features
have a meaningful order, although the differences between adjacent
levels should not be interpreted as equal numerical distances. Examples
include education level, satisfaction rating, and product tier. Binary
features are categorical features with exactly two levels, such as
yes/no, success/failure, or churn/no churn.

The distinction between numerical and categorical features guides the
choice of exploratory tools. Histograms, density plots, boxplots, and
numerical summaries are commonly used to examine numerical features.
Frequency tables and bar plots are generally more appropriate for
categorical features. Discrete numerical features with only a small
number of possible values may also be examined using bar plots because
their distributions are more naturally represented as counts.

The conceptual type and analytical role of a feature should not be
inferred solely from how it is stored in R. Numerical features are
commonly represented as \texttt{numeric} or \texttt{integer} vectors,
while categorical features may be stored as \texttt{factor} or
\texttt{character} vectors. However, a categorical feature may be
encoded numerically, an ordinal feature may be stored as an unordered
factor, and an identifier may be stored as an integer. Placeholder
values such as \texttt{"unknown"} or \texttt{999} may also represent
missing or unspecified information without being recognized as missing
by R. We should therefore interpret each feature using its substantive
meaning, conceptual type, analytical role, and technical representation
together.

In the \texttt{churn} case study later in this chapter, we apply these
distinctions when examining numerical and categorical features, the
customer identifier, placeholder categories, and features derived from
other measurements.

\subsection*{Distribution Shape and Measures of
Center}\label{distribution-shape-and-measures-of-center}

For numerical features, understanding the shape of the distribution is
an important part of exploratory analysis. A distribution may be
approximately symmetric, or it may be skewed when observations extend
farther in one direction than the other. Right-skewed distributions have
a longer tail toward larger values, whereas left-skewed distributions
have a longer tail toward smaller values.

Distribution shape also affects how measures of center should be
interpreted. The mean is sensitive to observations in the tails of a
distribution, whereas the median is less affected by extreme values. In
an approximately symmetric distribution, the mean and median are
typically close. In a skewed distribution, the mean is generally pulled
toward the longer tail, while the median remains closer to the center of
the ordered observations. The mode identifies the most common or most
densely concentrated value and, in a unimodal distribution, is located
near the peak. These relationships are illustrated in Figure
\ref{fig-eda-skew-type}.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=1\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{images/ch_eda_skew_type.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-eda-skew-type}Illustrative symmetric and skewed
distributions showing the relative positions of the mean, median, and
mode. In a symmetric unimodal distribution, the three measures of center
coincide. In a skewed distribution, the mean is pulled toward the longer
tail, while the median is less affected.}

\end{figure}%

Recognizing distribution shape helps determine which numerical summaries
and visualizations are most informative. It also provides context for
interpreting unusual observations, since values that appear extreme
relative to the center of a skewed distribution are not necessarily
erroneous. We return to these ideas when examining outliers and
implausible values in the next section and when exploring numerical
features in the \texttt{churn} case study in Section
\ref{sec-EDA-sec-numeric}.

\section{Identifying Outliers and Implausible
Values}\label{sec-eda-outliers}

Unusual observations are an important part of data understanding because
they may reveal data-quality problems, rare cases, or meaningful
variation in the population. They may arise from data-entry errors,
unusual measurement conditions, differences in the data-collection
process, or genuinely rare but informative events. Regardless of their
origin, unusual observations can strongly influence numerical summaries,
visualizations, statistical analyses, and predictive models.

The central challenge is not merely to identify extreme values, but to
determine what they represent. A useful distinction can be made among
\emph{outliers}, \emph{data errors}, and \emph{rare observations}. An
outlier is a value or observation that appears unusual relative to the
overall pattern of the data. A data error is a value that is
incompatible with the meaning of the feature, the measurement process,
or known logical constraints. A rare observation is unusual but valid
and may contain important information.

For example, a diamond width of zero millimeters is physically
impossible and indicates a problem with the recorded measurement. By
contrast, an unusually expensive diamond may be rare but entirely valid.
Similarly, an exceptionally large transaction amount in a customer
dataset may represent genuine customer behavior rather than a recording
error. Treating all extreme values as errors may remove meaningful
information, while retaining clearly implausible values may distort the
analysis.

Outlier identification should therefore be treated as a diagnostic
process rather than as an automatic rule for changing the data.
Numerical summaries and visualizations can identify observations that
deserve closer inspection, but their interpretation should be guided by
feature definitions, measurement units, relationships with other
features, the data-collection process, and relevant domain knowledge.

\subsection*{Detecting Unusual Values with Visual
Tools}\label{detecting-unusual-values-with-visual-tools}

Visualizations provide a natural starting point for identifying unusual
or implausible values. Different plots reveal different aspects of a
distribution. Boxplots summarize the central range of a numerical
feature and flag values far from that range. Histograms show how
frequently values occur across the full distribution and may reveal
skewness, gaps, spikes, or isolated observations. Scatter plots are
useful for examining whether a value that is unusual in one feature is
also inconsistent with related features.

A standard boxplot uses the interquartile range (IQR) to identify
potential outliers, as illustrated in Figure
\ref{fig-eda-simple-boxplot}. Let \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) denote the first
and third quartiles. The interquartile range measures the spread of the
middle 50\% of the observations and is defined as \[
\mathrm{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1.
\] The lower and upper outlier thresholds, often called the
\emph{fences}, are \[
Q_1 - 1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR}
\] and \[
Q_3 + 1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR},
\] respectively. The whiskers typically extend to the smallest and
largest observed values that fall within these fences. Observations
beyond the fences are displayed as individual points and are treated as
potential outliers.

This rule provides a useful screening tool, but it does not establish
that a flagged observation is erroneous. In strongly skewed or
heavy-tailed distributions, a boxplot may identify many valid
observations simply because they lie far from the central half of the
data. Any flagged values should therefore be investigated using
contextual information and related features before conclusions are
drawn.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.35\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{images/ch_eda_simple_boxplot.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-eda-simple-boxplot}A boxplot summarizes the central
distribution of a numerical feature. The whiskers extend to the most
extreme observations within 1.5 times the interquartile range from the
quartiles, while observations beyond these limits are displayed
individually as potential outliers.}

\end{figure}%

To illustrate visual identification of unusual values, we use the
\texttt{diamonds} dataset from the \textbf{ggplot2} package. Each
observation represents a diamond, and the features \texttt{x},
\texttt{y}, and \texttt{z} record its physical dimensions in
millimeters. We focus on \texttt{y}, which represents diamond width.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(ggplot2)}

\FunctionTok{data}\NormalTok{(diamonds)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We first compare a boxplot shown on the full scale with a zoomed view of
the central part of the distribution:

\begin{Shaded}

The full-scale boxplot shows that a small number of extreme values

Histograms provide a complementary view because they show how

The full-scale histogram shows that most widths are concentrated between
approximately 2 and 6 millimeters. The zoomed count scale reveals
several isolated values, including seven observations with a width of
zero and two unusually large values, one slightly above 30 millimeters
and another close to 60 millimeters.

A width of zero is physically impossible for a recorded diamond and
therefore differs conceptually from an ordinary statistical outlier. The
very large values also deserve closer investigation, but their position
in the distribution alone is not sufficient to determine whether they
are erroneous.

\subsection*{Investigating Unusual Observations in
Context}\label{investigating-unusual-observations-in-context}

An unusual value should rarely be interpreted by examining one feature
in isolation. Related measurements, logical constraints, and information
about the observation as a whole may help determine whether the value is
plausible.

We inspect the observations for which \texttt{y} is either zero or
greater than 30 millimeters:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{diamonds[diamonds}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{y }\SpecialCharTok{==} \DecValTok{0} \SpecialCharTok{|}\NormalTok{ diamonds}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{y }\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{30}\NormalTok{,}
  \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"carat"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cut"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"color"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"clarity"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"x"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"y"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"z"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"price"}\NormalTok{)]}
   \CommentTok{\# A tibble: 9 x 8}
\NormalTok{     carat cut       color clarity     x     y     z price}
     \SpecialCharTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{dbl}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}} \ErrorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{ord}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}}     \ErrorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{ord}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}} \ErrorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{ord}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}}   \ErrorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{dbl}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}} \ErrorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{dbl}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}} \ErrorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{dbl}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}} \ErrorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{int}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}}
   \DecValTok{1}  \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{    Very Good H     VS2      }\DecValTok{0}      \DecValTok{0}    \DecValTok{0}     \DecValTok{5139}
   \DecValTok{2}  \FloatTok{1.14}\NormalTok{ Fair      G     VS1      }\DecValTok{0}      \DecValTok{0}    \DecValTok{0}     \DecValTok{6381}
   \DecValTok{3}  \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{    Premium   H     SI2      }\FloatTok{8.09}  \FloatTok{58.9}  \FloatTok{8.06} \DecValTok{12210}
   \DecValTok{4}  \FloatTok{1.56}\NormalTok{ Ideal     G     VS2      }\DecValTok{0}      \DecValTok{0}    \DecValTok{0}    \DecValTok{12800}
   \DecValTok{5}  \FloatTok{1.2}\NormalTok{  Premium   D     VVS1     }\DecValTok{0}      \DecValTok{0}    \DecValTok{0}    \DecValTok{15686}
   \DecValTok{6}  \FloatTok{2.25}\NormalTok{ Premium   H     SI2      }\DecValTok{0}      \DecValTok{0}    \DecValTok{0}    \DecValTok{18034}
   \CommentTok{\# i 3 more rows}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The observations with \texttt{y\ =\ 0} also have zero values for the
other physical dimensions. This pattern strongly suggests that the
dimensions were not recorded correctly, rather than that the diamonds
genuinely had zero length, width, and depth. The unusually large values
of \texttt{y} are also inconsistent with the corresponding values of
\texttt{x} and \texttt{z}, making recording or measurement errors more
plausible than genuinely exceptional diamond sizes.

This example illustrates the value of cross-feature inspection. A value
may appear merely extreme when examined on its own but become clearly
implausible when compared with related measurements. Conversely, an
extreme observation may appear internally consistent and therefore
represent a valid rare case.

When investigating an unusual observation, several forms of evidence
should be considered together. Logical constraints can indicate whether
a value is physically or conceptually possible, while comparisons with
related features can reveal inconsistencies within the same observation.
The units and definitions of the measurements are also important, as is
information from the original data source or documentation. Domain
knowledge about the population or process being studied can provide
further context, and the presence of similar values in other
observations may help determine whether the case is isolated or part of
a broader pattern.

No observation should be removed or changed solely because it lies
beyond a boxplot threshold or appears in the tail of a histogram. During
data understanding and exploration, the objective is to identify,
investigate, and document unusual or implausible values. Decisions about
correcting values, recoding them as missing, transforming features,
using robust methods, or excluding observations are made later during
Data Preparation for Modeling.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Apply the same checks to \texttt{x} and \texttt{z}. Use
boxplots and histograms to identify unusual values, then compare all
three diamond dimensions. Which observations seem unusual but plausible,
and which appear physically implausible?
\end{quote}

In the following \texttt{churn} case study, we apply the same principles
to a practical data science problem. Numerical summaries and exploratory
graphics are used not merely to display the data, but to make customer
patterns visible, communicate relevant limitations, and identify
questions that may guide later statistical inference and predictive
modeling.

\section{\texorpdfstring{Case Study: Exploring the \texttt{churn}
Dataset}{Case Study: Exploring the churn Dataset}}\label{sec-eda-EDA-churn}

Data understanding and exploratory data analysis are most useful when
they are grounded in a real dataset and guided by a practical problem.
In this section, we use the \texttt{churn} dataset from the
\textbf{liver} package to examine customer attrition in a credit card
portfolio. The dataset contains demographic, account-related,
behavioral, and financial information about customers, together with a
binary target indicating whether a customer closed their account.

Our aim at this stage is not to build a predictive model or make causal
claims about why customers leave. Instead, we seek to understand the
structure and quality of the dataset, examine how customer
characteristics and behavior vary across churn outcomes, and identify
patterns or data issues that may deserve closer attention during later
statistical analysis and predictive modeling.

The case study follows the logic of the Data Science Workflow introduced
in Chapter \ref{sec-chapter-intro-data-science}. We begin by clarifying
the practical problem, acquiring and inspecting the data, and
identifying the types and analytical roles of the features. We then
assess data quality and explore categorical and numerical features and
relationships among them. Throughout the analysis, we combine numerical
summaries, visualizations, and contextual reasoning to distinguish what
is directly observed in the data from interpretations that would require
formal inference or additional evidence.

\subsection*{Problem Definition}\label{problem-definition}

Customer churn refers to the loss of customers over time. In this case
study, a customer is classified as having churned when they close their
credit card account. For a bank, customer attrition is an important
practical problem because retaining existing customers may be less
costly than acquiring new ones. Identifying customers who show signs of
disengagement may also help the bank investigate service problems and
design more targeted retention strategies.

The practical objective is therefore to understand which customer
characteristics and behavioral patterns are associated with account
closure. We examine whether churn differs across demographic groups,
account and service-related features, credit usage, transaction
activity, and changes in customer behavior over time. These patterns may
help identify features that deserve closer attention in later
statistical analysis or predictive modeling.

The available data are observational, so the analysis cannot establish
why a customer closes an account or whether changing a particular
feature would prevent churn. For example, frequent contact with customer
service may be associated with churn, but this does not imply that
contacting customer service causes customers to leave. Both may instead
reflect an unresolved problem or declining customer satisfaction.
Exploratory findings should therefore be interpreted as associations
that generate questions rather than as causal explanations.

At this stage, the goal is to develop a structured understanding of the
dataset, assess whether it is suitable for studying customer attrition,
and identify patterns and limitations that may guide later analysis. We
begin by acquiring the \texttt{churn} dataset and inspecting its
structure, dimensions, unit of analysis, and target feature.

\subsection*{Data Acquisition and Initial
Inspection}\label{data-acquisition-and-initial-inspection}

Although the focus of this case study is the \emph{Data Understanding
and Exploration} stage, we briefly revisit Data Acquisition to establish
the source, structure, and context of the data before beginning detailed
exploration. The \texttt{churn} dataset, available in the \textbf{liver}
package, contains demographic, account-related, behavioral, and
financial information about credit card customers. The target feature is
\texttt{churn}, which indicates whether a customer closed their credit
card account (\texttt{"yes"}) or remained active (\texttt{"no"}). At
this stage, the target is used to guide exploration rather than to build
a predictive model.

We begin by loading the package and dataset and inspecting its
structure:

    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ ratio\_count\_Q4\_Q1    }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ num  }\FloatTok{1.62} \FloatTok{3.71} \FloatTok{2.33} \FloatTok{2.33} \FloatTok{2.5}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ utilization\_ratio    }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ num  }\FloatTok{0.061} \FloatTok{0.105} \DecValTok{0} \FloatTok{0.76} \DecValTok{0} \FloatTok{0.311} \FloatTok{0.066} \FloatTok{0.048} \FloatTok{0.113} \FloatTok{0.144}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ churn                }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ Factor w}\SpecialCharTok{/} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{ levels }\StringTok{"yes"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"no"}\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{ ...}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The dataset is stored as a \texttt{data.frame} with 10127 observations
and 21 features. Each row represents one credit card customer,
establishing the customer as the unit of analysis. Each column records a
demographic characteristic, account attribute, or measure of customer
behavior or activity.

The features describe several aspects of the customer relationship.
Demographic features include \texttt{age}, \texttt{gender},
\texttt{education}, \texttt{marital}, \texttt{income}, and
\texttt{dependent\_count}. Account and relationship features include
\texttt{months\_on\_book}, \texttt{relationship\_count}, and
\texttt{card\_category}, while service-related behavior is represented
by \texttt{months\_inactive} and \texttt{contacts\_count\_12}. Credit
behavior is described by \texttt{credit\_limit},
\texttt{revolving\_balance}, \texttt{available\_credit}, and
\texttt{utilization\_ratio}. Transaction activity is summarized by
\texttt{transaction\_amount\_12}, \texttt{transaction\_count\_12},
\texttt{ratio\_amount\_Q4\_Q1}, and \texttt{ratio\_count\_Q4\_Q1}.

The dataset contains both categorical and numerical features.
Categorical features include \texttt{gender}, \texttt{education},
\texttt{marital}, \texttt{income}, \texttt{card\_category}, and the
binary target \texttt{churn}. Numerical features include measurements
such as \texttt{credit\_limit} and \texttt{transaction\_amount\_12}, as
well as discrete counts such as \texttt{dependent\_count},
\texttt{contacts\_count\_12}, and \texttt{transaction\_count\_12}.

The feature \texttt{customer\_ID} illustrates why technical
representation should not be confused with analytical meaning. Although
it is stored numerically in R, it serves as an account identifier rather
than as a quantitative measurement. Numerical summaries such as its mean
or standard deviation therefore have no substantive interpretation. Its
role is determined by what the feature represents, not by the fact that
R stores it as a number.

Some numerical features are derived from others. For example,
\texttt{available\_credit} is calculated from \texttt{credit\_limit} and
\texttt{revolving\_balance}, while \texttt{utilization\_ratio} expresses
revolving balance relative to credit limit. These derived features
summarize aspects of credit behavior, but their mathematical
relationships with their component features mean that they contain
overlapping information. We return to these relationships later when
examining associations and potential redundancy among features.

Initial inspection therefore involves more than identifying feature
names and R classes. It establishes the unit of analysis, clarifies the
target and other analytical roles, distinguishes conceptual feature
types from technical representations, and identifies features whose
meanings are linked by construction. With the basic structure and
interpretation of the dataset established, the next step is to assess
whether the recorded values raise any data-quality concerns.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Run \texttt{dim(churn)}, \texttt{names(churn)}, and
\texttt{head(churn)}. How does each function complement the information
provided by \texttt{str(churn)}? Identify the unit of analysis, the
target feature, the customer identifier, and at least one feature
derived from other measurements.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Assessing Data Quality}\label{assessing-data-quality}

Once the structure and analytical roles of the features are understood,
the next step is to assess the quality of the recorded data. At this
stage, we look for missing or unspecified information, implausible
values, and other indications that the data may not fully represent the
quantities or categories they are intended to measure. The objective is
to identify, investigate, and document such issues rather than decide
immediately how they should be handled.

We first use the \texttt{find.na()} function from the \textbf{liver}
package to check for values represented explicitly as \texttt{NA} in R:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{find.na}\NormalTok{(churn)}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\StringTok{" No missing values (NA) in the dataset."}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The output indicates that the dataset contains no values coded as
\texttt{NA}. This does not necessarily mean, however, that all
information is complete. Missing or unspecified values may be encoded
using placeholder categories or special numerical values that R treats
as ordinary observations. We therefore inspect selected categorical
features more closely:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(churn[, }\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"education"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"income"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"marital"}\NormalTok{)])}
\NormalTok{            education         income         marital    }
\NormalTok{    uneducated   }\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{1487}   \SpecialCharTok{\textless{}}\DecValTok{40}\NormalTok{K    }\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{3561}\NormalTok{   married }\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{4687}  
\NormalTok{    highschool   }\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{2013}   \DecValTok{40}\NormalTok{K}\DecValTok{{-}60}\NormalTok{K }\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{1790}\NormalTok{   single  }\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{3943}  
\NormalTok{    college      }\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{1013}   \DecValTok{60}\NormalTok{K}\DecValTok{{-}80}\NormalTok{K }\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{1402}\NormalTok{   divorced}\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{748}  
\NormalTok{    graduate     }\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{3128}   \DecValTok{80}\NormalTok{K}\DecValTok{{-}120}\NormalTok{K}\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{1535}\NormalTok{   unknown }\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{749}  
\NormalTok{    post}\SpecialCharTok{{-}}\NormalTok{graduate}\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{516}   \SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}}\DecValTok{120}\NormalTok{K   }\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{727}                  
\NormalTok{    doctorate    }\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{451}\NormalTok{   unknown }\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{1112}                  
\NormalTok{    unknown      }\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{1519}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The output shows that \texttt{education}, \texttt{income}, and
\texttt{marital} contain the level \texttt{"unknown"}. In this dataset,
\texttt{"unknown"} represents missing or unspecified information rather
than an ordinary substantive category. Because it is stored as a
categorical level rather than as \texttt{NA}, it is not detected by
\texttt{find.na()}.

During exploration, we retain \texttt{"unknown"} as an explicit level so
that these observations remain visible in summaries and visualizations.
This allows us to determine how frequently information is unspecified
and to examine whether the corresponding observations show patterns that
differ from those in the substantive categories. At this stage,
retaining \texttt{"unknown"} is an exploratory choice rather than a
final decision about how these values should be represented in later
analyses.

We also inspect the numerical features for unusual ranges and
potentially implausible values. The \texttt{summary()} function provides
a useful initial overview:
