The output reports the estimated coefficients, their standard errors,
the corresponding \emph{z}-statistics, and \emph{p}-values. Each
estimated coefficient \(b_j\) describes the direction and magnitude of
the relationship on the log-odds scale, while its standard error
reflects the uncertainty associated with that estimate. The
\emph{z}-statistic and \emph{p}-value provide evidence for assessing
whether the corresponding population coefficient \(\beta_j\) differs
from zero. As discussed in Chapters \ref{sec-chapter-statistics} and
\ref{sec-chapter-regression}, confidence intervals provide another way
to quantify uncertainty; in logistic regression, exponentiating their
endpoints gives confidence intervals for the corresponding odds ratios.

Each estimated coefficient in a fitted logistic regression model can be
interpreted on two closely related scales. On the model scale, the
estimated coefficient \(b_j\) describes the change in the log-odds of
loan approval associated with a one-unit increase in predictor \(x_j\),
holding the other predictors fixed. After exponentiation, the
coefficient can be interpreted as an \emph{odds ratio}. For a numeric
predictor \(x_j\), exponentiating the estimated coefficient \(b_j\)
gives \(e^{b_j}\), which represents the estimated multiplicative change
in the odds of loan approval associated with a one-unit increase in
\(x_j\), holding the other predictors fixed.

For example, according to the fitted model, the coefficient of
\texttt{loan\_term} is -0.152. The corresponding odds ratio is
\(e^{-0.152}\) = 0.859. This means that a one-unit increase in
\texttt{loan\_term} multiplies the odds of loan approval by about 0.859,
holding all other predictors fixed. If the odds ratio is greater than 1,
the predictor increases the odds of approval; if it is less than 1, the
predictor decreases the odds of approval.

For categorical predictors such as \texttt{education} or
\texttt{self\_employed}, the interpretation is relative to the reference
category. In that case, the exponentiated coefficient compares the odds
of loan approval in one category with the odds of loan approval in the
reference category, holding the other predictors fixed. More generally,
when factor variables are included in a model formula, R automatically
creates the required indicator variables and uses one level as the
reference category.

At this stage, we fit the model using the full dataset because our main
goal is to understand model specification and coefficient
interpretation. Later in this chapter, we return to logistic regression
in a predictive setting and evaluate its out-of-sample performance in a
fuller case study on predicting online purchase intention.

Taken together, these results show how logistic regression combines
model estimation with interpretable coefficient analysis, allowing us to
examine how individual predictors relate to the odds of loan approval.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Apply stepwise regression, as introduced in Section
\ref{sec-reg-stepwise}, to the logistic regression model. Compare the
selected model with the full model in terms of retained predictors and
interpretability. What does the reduced model suggest about the main
factors related to loan approval?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{From Estimated Probabilities to Classification
Decisions}\label{from-estimated-probabilities-to-classification-decisions}

A logistic regression model produces predicted probabilities rather than
class labels directly. These probabilities describe the estimated chance
that each observation belongs to the modeled event category. In many
applications, this probabilistic output is already useful, since it
allows us to rank observations by estimated risk or likelihood.

Predicted probabilities can be obtained using \texttt{predict()} with
\texttt{type\ =\ "response"}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{predict}\NormalTok{(glm\_loan, }\AttributeTok{newdata =}\NormalTok{ loan[}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, ], }\AttributeTok{type =} \StringTok{"response"}\NormalTok{), }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}
       \DecValTok{1}     \DecValTok{2}     \DecValTok{3}     \DecValTok{4}     \DecValTok{5} 
   \FloatTok{0.998} \FloatTok{0.078} \FloatTok{0.211} \FloatTok{0.420} \FloatTok{0.002}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

These values represent the model's estimated probabilities for the event
corresponding to the second level of \texttt{loan\_status}, which here
is approved. Since we set \texttt{"rejected"} as the reference category
in the previous subsection, the modeled event is loan approval. In other
words, these values give the estimated probability that each selected
loan application will be approved. For example, for the first
application in the \texttt{loan} dataset, the estimated probability of
approval is 0.998.

In some situations, predicted probabilities are the final quantity of
interest. In others, however, we need a class prediction such as
\texttt{approved} or \texttt{rejected}. To move from probabilities to
class labels, we choose a decision threshold. The most common choice is
0.5: if the predicted probability of approval is at least 0.5, we
classify the application as \texttt{approved}; otherwise, we classify it
as \texttt{rejected}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{loan\_probs }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{predict}\NormalTok{(glm\_loan, }\AttributeTok{newdata =}\NormalTok{ loan, }\AttributeTok{type =} \StringTok{"response"}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{loan\_pred\_05 }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{ifelse}\NormalTok{(loan\_probs }\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}=} \FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"approved"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"rejected"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{loan\_pred\_05 }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{factor}\NormalTok{(loan\_pred\_05, }\AttributeTok{levels =} \FunctionTok{levels}\NormalTok{(loan}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{loan\_status))}

\FunctionTok{table}\NormalTok{(loan\_pred\_05)}
\NormalTok{   loan\_pred\_05}
\NormalTok{   rejected approved }
       \DecValTok{1611}     \DecValTok{2658}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The threshold is applied to the probability of the modeled event. In
this example, the modeled event is loan approval, so lowering the
threshold makes it easier for an application to be classified as
\texttt{approved}, while raising the threshold makes the classification
rule more selective.

Although a threshold of 0.5 is common, it is not always the most
appropriate choice. The preferred threshold depends on the goals of the
application and the relative consequences of different types of errors.
In loan approval, for example, a lender may choose a higher threshold
for approval if the cost of approving a risky application is especially
high. Conversely, a lower threshold may be preferred if the cost of
rejecting applicants who would in fact repay the loan is considered
greater. The threshold should therefore reflect the practical balance
between caution and opportunity in the decision process. \emph{If the
threshold is chosen by comparing predictive performance across candidate
values, that choice should be made using training or validation data
rather than the final test set.}

This highlights one of the main strengths of logistic regression. It
separates the task of estimating probabilities from the task of making
decisions. The model provides estimated probabilities, and the analyst
selects a threshold that reflects the practical context. In the case
study later in this chapter, we evaluate probability-based classifiers
using ROC curves and the area under the curve, which allow us to assess
classification performance across all possible thresholds rather than
relying on a single cutoff.

Logistic regression therefore serves two closely related purposes. It is
a regression model for binary outcomes, and it is also a classification
tool that yields interpretable probabilities. This combination of
interpretability, flexibility, and practical usefulness explains why
logistic regression remains one of the most important methods for binary
data analysis.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Generate predicted probabilities for the \texttt{loan}
dataset and classify applications using thresholds of 0.5 and 0.3. How
does lowering the threshold affect the number of approvals and the
trade-off between approving risky applicants and rejecting applicants
who might repay the loan?
\end{quote}

\section{Poisson Regression for Count
Outcomes}\label{sec-glm-poisson-regression}

Not all response variables describe whether an event occurs. In many
applications, the outcome records \emph{how many times} something
happens within a fixed period or setting. Examples include the number of
doctor visits, the number of insurance claims, the number of purchases
made in a week, or the number of website visits in an hour. In Section
\ref{sec-reg-case-bike}, for example, we modeled hourly bike rental
demand using the variable \texttt{bike\_count}, which records the number
of bikes rented in each hour. Outcomes of this kind are not continuous
and are not simply binary. They are \emph{counts}, and they require a
model that respects their discrete, non-negative nature.

Poisson regression is one of the most important generalized linear
models for this setting. It extends the regression framework to
responses that represent event frequencies, allowing us to relate
expected counts to a set of predictors in a structured and interpretable
way. Just as logistic regression adapts regression to binary outcomes,
Poisson regression adapts it to count outcomes. Revisiting
\texttt{bike\_count} from Section \ref{sec-reg-case-bike} will therefore
help us see how a generalized linear model can sometimes provide a more
natural representation of a count response than ordinary linear
regression.

An important consideration in count modeling is the amount of
\emph{exposure} associated with each observation. The basic Poisson
regression model presented here is most directly applicable when
observations represent comparable periods or opportunities for events to
occur. When exposure differs, such as when individuals are observed for
different lengths of time, these differences can be incorporated into
the model, commonly through an offset. In the bike-demand example, each
observation represents one hour, so the exposure period is comparable
across observations.

This matters because ordinary linear regression is not well suited to
count data. A linear model can produce fitted values that are negative,
even though counts must be non-negative. It also assumes a constant
variance, whereas count outcomes often become more variable as their
expected value increases. In addition, count data are often
right-skewed, with many small values and fewer large ones. These
features make the normal-error framework of linear regression less
appropriate.

Poisson regression addresses these limitations by modeling the expected
count through a distribution and link function designed for count
outcomes. It is based on the Poisson distribution, named after the
French mathematician Siméon Denis Poisson (1781--1840), who studied
models for the number of events occurring within a fixed interval. If
\(Y\) follows a Poisson distribution with parameter \(\lambda > 0\),
then its probability mass function is \[
P(Y = y) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^y}{y!}, \qquad y = 0,1,2,\dots
\] where \(\lambda\) is the expected count. A key feature of the Poisson
distribution is that its mean and variance are both equal to
\(\lambda\): \[
\mathbb{E}(Y) = \lambda, \qquad \text{Var}(Y) = \lambda.
\]

To relate the expected count to predictors, Poisson regression uses the
\emph{log link}: \[
\log(\lambda) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_m x_m.
\] Here, \(\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_m\) denote the model
coefficients, following the same notation used for population regression
coefficients in Chapter \ref{sec-chapter-regression}. The model states
that the logarithm of the expected count is a linear function of the
predictors. Solving for \(\lambda\) gives \[
\lambda = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_m x_m}.
\]

This formulation guarantees that the expected count is always positive.
It also implies that predictors act multiplicatively on the original
count scale, even though their effects are additive on the log scale.
When the model is fitted to observed data, the unknown coefficients
\(\beta_j\) are estimated by coefficients denoted by \(b_j\), consistent
with the notation used in Chapter \ref{sec-chapter-regression}. In this
way, Poisson regression provides a statistically coherent and
interpretable framework for modeling count outcomes.

\subsection*{Fitting and Interpreting a Poisson Regression Model for
Bike
Demand}\label{fitting-and-interpreting-a-poisson-regression-model-for-bike-demand}

In Section \ref{sec-reg-case-bike}, we modeled hourly bike rental demand
using linear regression, including nonlinear terms and a square-root
transformation of the response. That analysis showed that linear
regression can provide a useful approximation for this problem. At the
same time, the response variable \texttt{bike\_count} records the number
of bike rentals in each hour, so it is fundamentally a count outcome.
This makes Poisson regression a natural alternative to consider.

To make the comparison with Section \ref{sec-reg-case-bike} meaningful,
we reproduce the same chronological training-test split used there.
Before creating the split, we perform only fixed operations that do not
depend on patterns observed in the response: we parse \texttt{date},
retain functioning days, order the observations chronologically by
\texttt{date} and \texttt{hour}, and derive \texttt{weekday} from the
calendar date. We then assign the first 80\% of the observations to the
training set and reserve the remaining 20\% as the test set.

The model-development choices made in Chapter
\ref{sec-chapter-regression} were based on the training data. These
included treating \texttt{hour} as a categorical predictor, using a
quadratic term for \texttt{temperature}, and applying a square-root
transformation to \texttt{bike\_count} for the linear regression model.
We reuse those established choices here so that the linear and Poisson
models are compared under a consistent modeling setup. The Poisson
model, however, is fitted directly to the original \texttt{bike\_count}
response because it models expected counts without requiring the
square-root transformation.

We now fit a Poisson regression model using the same candidate predictor
specification. Unlike the linear model, which models the square root of
\texttt{bike\_count}, the Poisson model uses the original count
response:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{formula\_full\_reg\_glm }\OtherTok{=}\NormalTok{ bike\_count }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ temperature }\SpecialCharTok{+} \FunctionTok{I}\NormalTok{(temperature}\SpecialCharTok{\^{}}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ humidity }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ wind\_speed }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ visibility }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ dew\_point\_temperature }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ solar\_radiation }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ rainfall }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ snowfall }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ season }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ holiday }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ hour }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ weekday}

\NormalTok{full\_reg\_glm }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{glm}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{formula =}\NormalTok{ formula\_full\_reg\_glm, }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ train\_bike, }\AttributeTok{family =}\NormalTok{ poisson)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The argument \texttt{family\ =\ poisson} tells R to use a Poisson
response distribution together with the default log link. The expected
number of bike rentals is therefore modeled directly as a positive
quantity. As an exploratory model-simplification step, we also apply the
stepwise procedure introduced in Chapter \ref{sec-chapter-regression}.
Importantly, this procedure uses only the training data:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{stepwise\_reg\_glm }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{step}\NormalTok{(full\_reg\_glm, }\AttributeTok{direction =} \StringTok{"both"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{trace =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The fitted model can be examined using
\texttt{summary(stepwise\_reg\_glm)}, which reports the estimated
coefficients, their standard errors, the corresponding
\emph{z}-statistics, and \emph{p}-values. Because the complete output is
lengthy, we do not reproduce it here. Instead, we focus on the
interpretation of the fitted coefficients.

For example, the estimated coefficient of \texttt{temperature} is 0.061.
Because Poisson regression uses the log link, this coefficient describes
the estimated change in the log of the expected bike count associated
with a one-unit increase in temperature, holding the remaining
predictors fixed. Exponentiating the coefficient gives 1.063, indicating
that a one-unit increase in temperature multiplies the expected number
of bike rentals by approximately this factor. Equivalently, this
corresponds to an estimated change of about 6.3\% in the expected count,
holding the other predictors fixed.

For categorical predictors, interpretation is relative to a reference
category. For example, the coefficient for \texttt{holidayno} compares
non-holidays with the reference category \texttt{holidayyes}, holding
the remaining predictors fixed. Exponentiating this coefficient gives
the estimated multiplicative difference in expected bike rentals between
non-holidays and holidays.

More generally, each estimated coefficient can be interpreted on two
related scales. For a numerical predictor \(x_j\), the estimated
coefficient \(b_j\) represents the change in the log of the expected
count associated with a one-unit increase in \(x_j\), holding the other
predictors fixed. Exponentiating the coefficient gives \(e^{b_j}\),
which represents the estimated factor by which the expected count
changes for a one-unit increase in \(x_j\).

After the model-development steps have been completed, we use the
reserved test set for final predictive evaluation. Predicted expected
counts from the stepwise Poisson model are obtained using
\texttt{predict()} with \texttt{type\ =\ "response"}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pred\_stepwise\_glm }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{predict}\NormalTok{(stepwise\_reg\_glm, }\AttributeTok{newdata =}\NormalTok{ test\_bike, }\AttributeTok{type =} \StringTok{"response"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

These values are the model's estimated expected numbers of bike rentals
for the test observations. Because Poisson regression predicts expected
counts, the predicted values do not need to be integers. They represent
expected demand rather than the realized number of rentals in a
particular hour.

We can now compare the Poisson regression model with the linear
regression model from Section \ref{sec-reg-case-bike} on the original
\texttt{bike\_count} scale. For the linear model, predictions are first
obtained on the square-root scale and then transformed back to the
original count scale. We summarize predictive performance using RMSE and
predictive \(R^2\):

\begin{verbatim}
                      Model     RMSE        R2
   1  Stepwise linear model 333.8172 0.6897669
   2 Stepwise Poisson model 289.1020 0.7673125
\end{verbatim}

In this setting, the stepwise Poisson model achieves a lower predictive
RMSE and a higher predictive \(R^2\) than the stepwise linear model from
Chapter \ref{sec-chapter-regression}. In particular, the predictive RMSE
decreases from about 333.8 to about 289.1, while the predictive \(R^2\)
increases from about 0.69 to about 0.77. These results suggest that
modeling \texttt{bike\_count} directly as a count outcome provides a
more effective representation for this particular prediction problem.

Figure \ref{fig-glm-bike-poisson-vs-linear} compares observed and
predicted bike rentals for the stepwise linear model from Chapter
\ref{sec-reg-case-bike} and the stepwise Poisson model. The Poisson
model produces predictions that track the diagonal reference line more
closely, which is consistent with its improved predictive performance on
the test set. At the same time, Poisson regression should still be
viewed as a starting point rather than a final answer for every
count-data problem. Hourly demand data may exhibit overdispersion,
meaning that the variability in the response exceeds what the Poisson
model assumes. If substantial overdispersion is present, alternatives
such as quasi-Poisson or negative binomial regression may be considered
(Dobson and Barnett 2018). These extensions are beyond the main scope of
this introductory chapter. It is therefore important to check model
adequacy in practice, even when Poisson regression performs better than
ordinary linear regression.

\begin{figure}

\centering{

\begin{figure}[H]

\begin{minipage}{0.50\linewidth}
\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{9-generalized-regression_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-14-1.pdf}}\end{minipage}%
%
\begin{minipage}{0.50\linewidth}
\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{9-generalized-regression_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-14-2.pdf}}\end{minipage}%

\end{figure}%

}

\caption{\label{fig-glm-bike-poisson-vs-linear}Observed versus predicted
bike rentals for the stepwise linear regression model and the stepwise
Poisson regression model.}

\end{figure}%

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Revisit the \texttt{bike\_demand} analysis in Section
\ref{sec-reg-case-bike} and compare the stepwise linear and Poisson
regression models. Interpret one numerical and one categorical predictor
from the Poisson model on the log and expected-count scales. How does
this interpretation differ from that of the linear regression model?
\end{quote}

\section{Case Study: Predicting Online Purchase Intention with Logistic
Regression}\label{sec-glm-case-study}

Predicting whether an online browsing session will end in a purchase is
a common classification problem in e-commerce. Accurate probability
estimates can help businesses identify sessions with high conversion
potential, target promotions more effectively, and better understand the
factors related to customer purchasing behavior. In this case study, we
ask a focused question: can an interpretable logistic regression model
provide competitive probability-based predictions for online purchase
intention?

The \texttt{purchase\_intention} dataset comes from the UC Irvine
Machine Learning Repository and is distributed with the liver package.
It was described by Sakar et al. (2019) in the context of predicting
online purchasing behavior. The response variable, \texttt{revenue},
records whether a session resulted in a completed transaction, while the
predictors describe browsing behavior, session-level characteristics,
and visitor-related features. This makes the dataset well suited for
illustrating logistic regression in a realistic binary classification
setting.

Following the Data Science Workflow introduced in Chapter
\ref{sec-chapter-intro-data-science} and illustrated in
Figure~\ref{fig-ds_DSW}, this case study proceeds from problem
definition and data acquisition to data understanding and exploration,
data preparation for modeling, modeling, and model evaluation. We first
examine the \texttt{purchase\_intention} data and establish the
training-test split. Using the training data, we then fit a baseline
logistic regression model, followed by a stepwise logistic regression
model, and include the Naive Bayes classifier from Chapter
\ref{sec-chapter-bayes} as a benchmark based on a different modeling
principle. Once the models have been finalized, we compare their
probability-based predictions on the reserved test set. The comparison
considers predictive performance together with interpretability and
parsimony.

\subsection*{Problem Definition}\label{problem-definition-2}

Online retailers routinely seek to understand which browsing sessions
are most likely to end in a purchase. Identifying sessions with a high
probability of conversion can help businesses target promotions more
effectively, improve recommendation strategies, allocate marketing
resources, and refine website design. This makes purchase intention a
natural prediction problem in e-commerce: given information recorded
during a browsing session, can we estimate whether that session will
generate revenue?

From a modeling perspective, this is a binary classification problem.
The outcome variable \texttt{revenue} records whether a session ended in
a purchase (\texttt{yes}) or not (\texttt{no}). The predictors include
behavioral variables, such as the number of pages visited and the time
spent on different types of pages, together with session-level and
visitor-level characteristics such as \texttt{month},
\texttt{visitor\_type}, \texttt{traffic\_type}, and \texttt{weekend}.
Our aim is to estimate the probability of purchase for each session
while also considering the trade-off between predictive performance and
interpretability. For this reason, we begin with logistic regression,
then consider a stepwise logistic regression model, and finally compare
these models with Naive Bayes as an external benchmark.

\subsection*{Overview of the Dataset}\label{overview-of-the-dataset}

The \texttt{purchase\_intention} dataset is available through the
\textbf{liver} package. We begin by loading the data and examining its
structure, covering the Data Acquisition and Data Understanding and
Exploration stages of the Data Science Workflow. Each observation
corresponds to a single browsing session, and the modeling objective is
to predict whether that session ended in a purchase
(\texttt{revenue\ =\ "yes"} or \texttt{"no"}). The dataset combines
behavioral measures with session-level and visitor-related
characteristics, making it well suited for supervised classification in
an e-commerce setting.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(liver)}

\FunctionTok{data}\NormalTok{(purchase\_intention)}

\FunctionTok{str}\NormalTok{(purchase\_intention)}
   \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}data.frame\textquotesingle{}}\SpecialCharTok{:}    \DecValTok{12330}\NormalTok{ obs. of  }\DecValTok{18}\NormalTok{ variables}\SpecialCharTok{:}
    \ErrorTok{$}\NormalTok{ administrative          }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ int  }\DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{ ...}

    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ product\_related\_duration}\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ num  }\DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{64} \DecValTok{0} \FloatTok{2.67} \FloatTok{627.5}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ bounce\_rates            }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ num  }\FloatTok{0.2} \DecValTok{0} \FloatTok{0.2} \FloatTok{0.05} \FloatTok{0.02}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ exit\_rates              }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ num  }\FloatTok{0.2} \FloatTok{0.1} \FloatTok{0.2} \FloatTok{0.14} \FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ page\_values             }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ num  }\DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{ ...}

    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ browser                 }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ Factor w}\SpecialCharTok{/} \DecValTok{13}\NormalTok{ levels }\StringTok{"1"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"2"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"3"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"4"}\NormalTok{,..}\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{4} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{ ...}

    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ traffic\_type            }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ Factor w}\SpecialCharTok{/} \DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{ levels }\StringTok{"1"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"2"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"3"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"4"}\NormalTok{,..}\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{4} \DecValTok{4} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{5} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ visitor\_type            }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ Factor w}\SpecialCharTok{/} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{ levels }\StringTok{"New\_Visitor"}\NormalTok{,..}\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ weekend                 }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ Factor w}\SpecialCharTok{/} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{ levels }\StringTok{"no"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"yes"}\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ revenue                 }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ Factor w}\SpecialCharTok{/} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{ levels }\StringTok{"no"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"yes"}\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{ ...}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The dataset consists of 12330 observations and 18 variables. The
response variable, \texttt{revenue}, is binary and indicates whether the
session resulted in a completed transaction. The predictors describe
several aspects of the browsing session. Some variables summarize
browsing behavior, including the number of administrative,
informational, and product-related pages visited and the time spent on
each type of page. Others capture session quality and commercial
relevance, such as \texttt{bounce\_rates}, \texttt{exit\_rates},
\texttt{page\_values}, and \texttt{special\_day}. Additional variables
describe session and visitor characteristics, including \texttt{month},
\texttt{weekend}, \texttt{visitor\_type}, \texttt{traffic\_type},
\texttt{region}, \texttt{browser}, and \texttt{operating\_systems}.

Taken together, these predictors provide a rich description of online
shopping sessions and the conditions under which purchases occur. For
this case study, the dataset is already stored in an analysis-ready
format, with categorical variables represented as factors and the binary
outcome clearly defined. As a result, no additional cleaning is required
before proceeding to Data Preparation for Modeling, where we establish
the training-test split for model development and final evaluation.

\subsection*{Data Preparation for
Modeling}\label{data-preparation-for-modeling-3}

To evaluate how well the models generalize to new data, we divide the
\texttt{purchase\_intention} dataset into separate training and test
sets. The training set is used for model development, while the test set
is reserved for final out-of-sample evaluation. This separation allows
predictive performance to be assessed on observations that were not used
when fitting or selecting the models.

Following the approach used elsewhere in the book, we use the
\texttt{partition()} function from the \textbf{liver} package to create
an 80\% training set and a 20\% test set. We also set a random seed to
make the partition reproducible:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{set.seed}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{42}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{splits }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{partition}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ purchase\_intention, }\AttributeTok{ratio =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{train\_set }\OtherTok{=}\NormalTok{ splits}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{part1}
\NormalTok{test\_set  }\OtherTok{=}\NormalTok{ splits}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{part2}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The split assigns most observations to the training set while leaving a
substantial subset for model evaluation. Because \texttt{revenue} is the
response variable, it is useful to check descriptively whether its class
proportions are reasonably similar across the training and test sets:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{prop.table}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{table}\NormalTok{(train\_set}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{revenue))}
   
\NormalTok{          no       yes }
   \FloatTok{0.8437753} \FloatTok{0.1562247}
\FunctionTok{prop.table}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{table}\NormalTok{(test\_set}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{revenue))}
   
\NormalTok{         no      yes }
   \FloatTok{0.851176} \FloatTok{0.148824}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The proportions indicate that the class distribution is similar across
the two subsets. This descriptive check helps identify whether the
random partition has produced an unusually different class balance in
the test set. A formal hypothesis test is neither necessary nor
appropriate for this purpose because the objective is to inspect the
partition rather than test a population-level hypothesis.

No additional preprocessing is required for the models considered in
this case study. The categorical predictors are already represented as
factors, and the numerical predictors are ready for direct use. We
therefore proceed to the Modeling stage using the training data, while
keeping the test set reserved for final evaluation.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Repeat the partition using a 70\% training set and a
30\% test set. Compare the class proportions of \texttt{revenue} across
the resulting subsets. How does changing the partitioning ratio affect
the amount of data available for model development and final evaluation?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Fitting the Baseline Logistic Regression
Model}\label{fitting-the-baseline-logistic-regression-model}

We begin with logistic regression, which serves as the main modeling
approach in this case study. Logistic regression is a natural choice
because the response variable is binary and the goal is to estimate the
probability that an online browsing session ends in a purchase.

We fit a baseline logistic regression model using all available
predictors in the training set. In \texttt{glm()}, the argument
\texttt{family\ =\ binomial} specifies a logistic regression model for a
binary response using the logit link:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{baseline\_logit }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{glm}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{formula =}\NormalTok{ revenue }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ train\_set,}\AttributeTok{family =}\NormalTok{ binomial)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The baseline model provides a reference specification that includes all
available predictors. At this stage, our focus is on model development
using the training data. We therefore do not yet generate predictions
for the test set. Those predictions will be obtained only after all
models have been finalized and will be used for final out-of-sample
comparison in the Model Evaluation and Comparison subsection.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Inspect \texttt{summary(baseline\_logit)}. Which
predictors have positive or negative associations with the log-odds of
purchase? Treat these patterns as in-sample model interpretation rather
than out-of-sample performance.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Fitting the Stepwise Logistic Regression
Model}\label{fitting-the-stepwise-logistic-regression-model}

The baseline logistic regression model includes all available
predictors. While this provides a natural starting point, in practice we
often ask whether a simpler model may provide a more parsimonious
representation. A reduced model can be easier to interpret, easier to
communicate, and more practical to use.

To investigate this possibility, we apply stepwise selection to the
baseline logistic regression model using the training data. Stepwise
selection compares a sequence of candidate models by adding or removing
predictors and evaluating them using the Akaike Information Criterion
(AIC). As discussed in Section \ref{sec-reg-stepwise}, smaller AIC
values indicate a better balance between model fit and model complexity.
Here, we use bidirectional stepwise selection, which allows predictors
to be both added and removed during the search.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{stepwise\_logit }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{step}\NormalTok{(baseline\_logit, }\AttributeTok{direction =} \StringTok{"both"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{trace =} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The resulting model is a reduced version of the baseline logistic
regression model. Because stepwise selection is part of model
development, it is performed entirely using the training data. We do not
yet generate predictions for the test set. After all models have been
finalized, the reserved test set will be used to compare their
out-of-sample performance.

Stepwise selection should be interpreted cautiously. It is a data-driven
search procedure, so the selected model can be sensitive to small
changes in the data, and the usual coefficient summaries should not be
interpreted as if the model had been specified in advance. In this case
study, we use stepwise selection mainly as an exploratory tool for model
simplification, not as a guarantee of better predictive performance or
as a definitive procedure for identifying the true set of relevant
predictors.

The final evaluation will show whether the reduced model retains similar
discriminatory performance to the baseline logistic regression model. If
it does, the more compact specification may offer a useful practical
advantage through greater interpretability and parsimony.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Inspect the final stepwise model using
\texttt{formula(stepwise\_logit)} or \texttt{summary(stepwise\_logit)}.
Which predictors were retained, and how does the model differ from the
baseline logistic regression model? Why should the selected model be
interpreted cautiously?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Fitting the Naive Bayes
Model}\label{fitting-the-naive-bayes-model}

To broaden the comparison beyond logistic regression, we also fit a
Naive Bayes classifier. This model was introduced in Chapter
\ref{sec-chapter-bayes} and provides a useful external benchmark because
it is based on a different modeling principle. Whereas logistic
regression models the probability of the outcome through the log-odds,
Naive Bayes combines Bayes' rule with a simplifying assumption about the
predictors.

The defining assumption of Naive Bayes is that the predictors are
conditionally independent given the class label. In practice, this
assumption is often unrealistic, especially in a dataset such as
\texttt{purchase\_intention}, where behavioral variables such as page
counts, browsing durations, and engagement measures are likely to be
related. Even so, Naive Bayes often performs surprisingly well and is
widely used as a simple and computationally efficient benchmark in
classification problems.

We fit the model using the \texttt{naive\_bayes()} function from the
\textbf{naivebayes} package. As in the logistic regression models, we
use \texttt{revenue} as the response variable and include all available
predictors:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(naivebayes)}

\NormalTok{bayes\_fit }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{naive\_bayes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{formula =}\NormalTok{ revenue }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ ., }\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ train\_set, }\AttributeTok{laplace =} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The argument \texttt{laplace\ =\ 1} applies Laplace smoothing, which
helps avoid zero estimated probabilities when some predictor values
occur rarely within a class. At this stage, the Naive Bayes model is
fitted using the training data only. We do not yet generate predictions
for the test set. After all three models have been finalized, their
probability-based predictions will be obtained on the reserved test set
and compared using ROC curves and AUC in the Model Evaluation and
Comparison subsection.

Naive Bayes is interpretable in a different sense from logistic
regression: it summarizes how predictor distributions differ by class.
However, it does not provide coefficient-based effect estimates or odds
ratios. In this case study, its main role is to serve as a simple and
computationally efficient benchmark based on assumptions that differ
from those of logistic regression.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Many predictors in \texttt{purchase\_intention}, such
as page counts and browsing durations, are likely to be correlated. Why
does this create tension with the conditional independence assumption of
Naive Bayes? Compare this with the assumptions made by logistic
regression.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Model Evaluation and
Comparison}\label{model-evaluation-and-comparison}

We now evaluate the three finalized models on the reserved test set. At
this stage, the model specifications and all model-development decisions
have already been determined using the training data. The test set is
used only for final out-of-sample assessment; we do not revise predictor
sets, classification thresholds, or other modeling choices after
examining test performance. This preserves the role of the test set
described in Chapter \ref{sec-chapter-evaluation}.

We first store the true test-set labels and generate predicted
probabilities from each of the three models:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{test\_labels }\OtherTok{=}\NormalTok{ test\_set}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{revenue}

\NormalTok{baseline\_probs }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{predict}\NormalTok{(baseline\_logit, }\AttributeTok{newdata =}\NormalTok{ test\_set, }\AttributeTok{type =} \StringTok{"response"}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{stepwise\_probs }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{predict}\NormalTok{(stepwise\_logit, }\AttributeTok{newdata =}\NormalTok{ test\_set, }\AttributeTok{type =} \StringTok{"response"}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{bayes\_probs }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{predict}\NormalTok{(bayes\_fit, }\AttributeTok{newdata =}\NormalTok{ test\_set, }\AttributeTok{type =} \StringTok{"prob"}\NormalTok{)[, }\StringTok{"yes"}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For the two logistic regression models, \texttt{type\ =\ "response"}
returns the estimated probability that \texttt{revenue\ =\ "yes"}. For
the Naive Bayes model, \texttt{predict(...,\ type\ =\ "prob")} returns
probabilities for both outcome classes, so we select the \texttt{"yes"}
column. These probability-based predictions allow the three models to be
compared using the same evaluation framework.

The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive
rate as the classification threshold varies. The AUC summarizes this
curve into a single measure of discriminatory performance: values closer
to 1 indicate stronger separation between the two outcome classes.
Because \texttt{purchase\_intention} is imbalanced, precision-recall
curves can also provide a useful perspective on classifier performance.
Here, however, we focus on ROC curves and AUC to compare discriminatory
performance across thresholds for the three models.

We compute the ROC curves using the \textbf{pROC} package:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(pROC)}

\NormalTok{roc\_logistic }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{roc}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{response =}\NormalTok{ test\_labels, }\AttributeTok{predictor =}\NormalTok{ baseline\_probs)}
\NormalTok{roc\_stepwise }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{roc}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{response =}\NormalTok{ test\_labels, }\AttributeTok{predictor =}\NormalTok{ stepwise\_probs)}
\NormalTok{roc\_bayes    }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{roc}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{response =}\NormalTok{ test\_labels, }\AttributeTok{predictor =}\NormalTok{ bayes\_probs)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To compare the models visually, we plot all three ROC curves in a single
figure:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{ggroc}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{list}\NormalTok{(roc\_logistic, roc\_stepwise, roc\_bayes), }\AttributeTok{size =} \FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{scale\_color\_manual}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{values =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"\#377EB8"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"\#4DAF4A"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"\#E66101"}\NormalTok{),}
    \AttributeTok{labels =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{paste}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Logistic (AUC ="}\NormalTok{, }\FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{auc}\NormalTok{(roc\_logistic), }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{), }\StringTok{")"}\NormalTok{),}
        \FunctionTok{paste}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Stepwise (AUC ="}\NormalTok{, }\FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{auc}\NormalTok{(roc\_stepwise), }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{), }\StringTok{")"}\NormalTok{),}
        \FunctionTok{paste}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Naive Bayes (AUC ="}\NormalTok{, }\FunctionTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{auc}\NormalTok{(roc\_bayes), }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{), }\StringTok{")"}\NormalTok{))) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{ggtitle}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"ROC Curves for Three Classification Models"}\NormalTok{) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{theme}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{legend.title =} \FunctionTok{element\_blank}\NormalTok{(), }\AttributeTok{legend.position =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(.}\DecValTok{72}\NormalTok{, .}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.9\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{9-generalized-regression_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-23-1.pdf}
\end{center}

The ROC curves allow us to compare the models across a range of
thresholds rather than at a single cutoff. In this case, the baseline
logistic regression model and the stepwise logistic regression model
achieve very similar AUC values, suggesting that the reduced model
preserves most of the discriminatory information contained in the full
model. This is a practically useful result, since a simpler model may
offer nearly the same discriminatory performance while being easier to
interpret and communicate.

Naive Bayes provides a useful external benchmark. Its performance shows
whether a classifier based on a different modeling principle remains
competitive on this dataset. Even with its simplifying conditional
independence assumption, Naive Bayes can still provide a meaningful
benchmark for comparison.

Taken together, the results illustrate a common applied trade-off. The
baseline logistic regression model provides an interpretable reference
point, the stepwise model examines whether a more parsimonious
specification is sufficient, and Naive Bayes offers a contrasting
benchmark. Comparing all three helps us evaluate not only discriminatory
performance, but also interpretability, parsimony, and practical
usefulness.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Compare the AUC values of the three models and
interpret the differences. If two models achieve very similar AUC
values, what considerations other than predictive performance might
guide the choice between them?
\end{quote}

\section{Chapter Summary and Takeaways}\label{sec-glm-summary}

In this chapter, we extended the regression framework beyond continuous
outcomes by introducing generalized linear models. The central idea is
to match the model to the structure of the response variable. A GLM
combines a response distribution, a linear predictor, and a link
function, allowing regression methods to be adapted to outcomes such as
binary responses and counts.

For binary outcomes, we studied logistic regression. This model uses the
logit link to relate predictors to the log-odds of an event while
ensuring that predicted probabilities remain between 0 and 1. Logistic
regression is therefore useful both as an interpretable regression model
and as a classification tool. Its coefficients can be interpreted
through odds ratios, and its predicted probabilities can be converted
into class predictions when a decision threshold is required.

For count outcomes, we studied Poisson regression. This model uses the
log link to relate predictors to the expected count and allows predictor
effects to be interpreted multiplicatively on the original count scale.
Poisson regression also relies on assumptions that should be assessed in
practice, particularly the relationship between the mean and variance.
Substantial overdispersion may indicate that alternatives such as
quasi-Poisson or negative binomial regression should be considered.

The case study on online purchase intention illustrated how logistic
regression can be used in a predictive setting. By comparing the
baseline logistic regression model, the stepwise logistic regression
model, and Naive Bayes using ROC curves and AUC, we emphasized that
model choice should not depend on predictive performance alone.
Interpretability, parsimony, and the decision context also influence the
choice of a useful model. This reinforces a broader message of the Data
Science Workflow: effective modeling requires matching the method not
only to the structure of the data, but also to the purpose of the
analysis.

Chapter \ref{sec-chapter-trees} moves from generalized linear models to
decision trees and random forests. Unlike the regression-based models
developed in Chapters \ref{sec-chapter-regression} and
\ref{sec-chapter-glm}, tree-based methods can capture nonlinear
relationships and interactions through recursive partitioning.

\section{Exercises}\label{sec-glm-exercises}

These exercises reinforce the main ideas of the chapter through
conceptual questions and practical applications in R. They focus on
logistic regression, Poisson regression, and model comparison using
datasets from the \textbf{liver} package.

\subsubsection*{Conceptual
Understanding}\label{conceptual-understanding}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Explain why ordinary linear regression is not appropriate for a binary
  response variable.
\item
  Explain why ordinary linear regression is not appropriate for count
  data.
\item
  What are the three main components of a generalized linear model?
\item
  What is the role of a link function in a generalized linear model?
\item
  Why does logistic regression use the logit link rather than the
  identity link?
\item
  Why does Poisson regression use the log link rather than the identity
  link?
\item
  What is an odds ratio, and how is it interpreted in logistic
  regression?
\item
  In Poisson regression, what does \(e^{\beta_j}\) represent for a
  predictor \(x_j\)?
\item
  What is overdispersion in the context of Poisson regression, and why
  can it be problematic?
\item
  Logistic regression and Poisson regression are both generalized linear
  models. What do they have in common, and how do they differ?
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection*{\texorpdfstring{Hands-On Practice: Logistic Regression
with the \texttt{loan}
Dataset}{Hands-On Practice: Logistic Regression with the loan Dataset}}\label{hands-on-practice-logistic-regression-with-the-loan-dataset}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{data}\NormalTok{(loan, }\AttributeTok{package =} \StringTok{"liver"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{10}
\item
  Inspect the structure of the \texttt{loan} dataset. Which variable is
  the response, and which variables are plausible predictors?
\item
  Define loan approval as the modeled event by setting
  \texttt{"rejected"} as the reference category of
  \texttt{loan\_status}. Fit a logistic regression model using
  \texttt{income\_annum}, \texttt{loan\_amount}, and
  \texttt{cibil\_score}.
\item
  Inspect the fitted model using \texttt{summary()}. Interpret the
  estimated coefficient for \texttt{cibil\_score} in terms of the
  log-odds of loan approval.
\item
  Exponentiate the estimated coefficients. Interpret the odds ratio for
  \texttt{cibil\_score} in the context of loan approval.
\item
  Extend the model by adding \texttt{education} and
  \texttt{self\_employed}. How do the coefficient estimates and their
  statistical significance change?
\item
  Use the extended model to estimate the probability of approval for an
  applicant with \texttt{income\_annum\ =\ 5000000},
  \texttt{loan\_amount\ =\ 12000000}, \texttt{cibil\_score\ =\ 750},
  \texttt{education\ =\ "Graduate"}, and
  \texttt{self\_employed\ =\ "No"}.
\item
  Use \texttt{partition()} to create an 80\% training set and a 20\%
  test set. Fit the extended logistic regression model using the
  training data only.
\item
  Apply stepwise selection using the training data. Which predictors are
  retained, and how does the selected model differ from the full model?
  Why should the selected model be interpreted cautiously?
\item
  Generate test-set probabilities from the full model and classify
  observations using thresholds of 0.5 and 0.3. Compare the resulting
  confusion matrices. How does lowering the threshold affect the
  classification errors?
\item
  Using a threshold of 0.5, compute accuracy, precision, recall, and
  F1-score on the test set for the full and stepwise models. Compare
  their out-of-sample performance, interpretability, and parsimony.
\end{enumerate}
