code. The namespace operator \texttt{::} specifies the package from
which a function should be used. For example,
\texttt{liver::partition()} calls the \texttt{partition()} function from
the \textbf{liver} package. This notation can be useful when different
packages contain functions with the same name or when the package
dependency should be made explicit.

Pipe operators provide another way to write sequences of operations. The
base R pipe \texttt{\textbar{}\textgreater{}} passes the result of one
expression to the next function, allowing code to be read from left to
right. Readers may also encounter \texttt{\%\textgreater{}\%}, a pipe
operator commonly used with packages such as \textbf{dplyr}. Pipes are
not essential at this stage, but recognizing them makes it easier to
read examples, documentation, and existing R code. Throughout the book,
these operators are used only when they improve readability.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Define \texttt{x\ =\ 7} and \texttt{y\ =\ 5}. Compute
\texttt{x\ +\ y}, \texttt{x\ \textgreater{}\ y}, and
\texttt{(x\ \textgreater{}\ 1)\ \&\ (y\ \textless{}\ 5)}. Then change
the values of \texttt{x} and \texttt{y} and evaluate the expressions
again.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Functions in R}\label{functions-in-r}

Functions are central to working with R. They allow common tasks to be
expressed concisely, such as combining values, calculating summary
statistics, transforming data, and producing visualizations. A function
typically takes one or more \emph{arguments}, performs a task, and
returns an output.

For example, the \texttt{c()} function, short for ``combine,'' creates a
vector by combining individual values:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{prices }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{37}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{61}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Once this vector has been created, other functions can be applied to it.
For example, \texttt{sum()} calculates the total of the values, while
\texttt{mean()} calculates their average:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{sum}\NormalTok{(prices)}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\DecValTok{100}

\FunctionTok{mean}\NormalTok{(prices)}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\FloatTok{33.33333}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The general structure of a function call in R is:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{function\_name}\NormalTok{(argument1, argument2, ...)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The values supplied inside the parentheses are called \emph{arguments}.
Some arguments are required for a function to work, while others are
optional and have default values. The specific arguments available
depend on the function being used, but the same basic structure applies
throughout R.

Functions are often combined with objects and operators to perform more
useful analytical tasks. As code becomes more detailed, comments can
help explain the purpose of individual steps and make the analysis
easier to follow.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Create a vector called \texttt{scores} containing the
values 70, 85, 90, and 75 using \texttt{c()}. Then use \texttt{sum()} to
calculate the total and \texttt{mean()} to calculate the average. Modify
one of the values and run the functions again to observe how the results
change.
\end{quote}

\section{Getting Help and Learning
More}\label{getting-help-and-learning-more}

Questions, errors, and unexpected output are a normal part of learning
R. A useful first step when something is unclear is to check what a
function is designed to do, which arguments it accepts, and what output
it returns. R's built-in documentation therefore provides an important
starting point for troubleshooting and learning unfamiliar functions.

The simplest way to open a help page is to type a question mark followed
by the function name. The \texttt{help()} function provides the same
documentation, while \texttt{example()} runs examples included with the
function. For instance, the following commands provide information and
examples for \texttt{mean()}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{?mean}
\FunctionTok{help}\NormalTok{(mean)}
\FunctionTok{example}\NormalTok{(mean)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Help pages typically describe a function's purpose, arguments, returned
values, and examples of its use. Many R packages also provide
\emph{vignettes}, which offer more detailed explanations and demonstrate
how several functions can be used together. These resources are
particularly useful when learning packages used throughout this book,
such as \textbf{ggplot2} and \textbf{liver}.

When built-in documentation is not sufficient, external resources such
as Stack Overflow and the Posit Community can help with common errors
and practical coding questions. AI-based assistants can also help
explain error messages, clarify syntax, or suggest small examples.
However, suggested code should be checked against the relevant
documentation, the structure of the data, and the purpose of the
analysis. Code may run without producing an error while still being
inappropriate for the intended task.

When seeking help, it is useful to provide a small reproducible example
whenever possible. This typically includes the relevant code, the error
message or unexpected output, and enough information about the data for
the problem to be understood. Developing this habit makes
troubleshooting more effective and supports clear, reproducible
analysis.

\section{Loading and Importing Data in R}\label{sec-R-import-data}

Before data can be explored, visualized, or modeled in R, it must first
be made available in the current R session. Loading or importing data is
one of the practical activities associated with the Data Acquisition
stage of the Data Science Workflow. Data can enter an analysis in
several ways. Some datasets are included in R packages, while others are
stored in external files such as CSV or Excel files. Package datasets
provide a convenient and reproducible way to work with example data,
whereas external files reflect how data are often encountered in
practice.

Whenever possible, the data-loading step should be made explicit in code
so that the analysis can be rerun, checked, and shared. For this reason,
we begin with datasets loaded from R packages, which provide a simple
and reproducible entry point. We then introduce RStudio's graphical
import interface as a useful beginner tool before turning to code-based
import from CSV and Excel files. Although the graphical interface can
help users understand import settings interactively, the generated code
should be saved when the analysis needs to be repeated or shared.

\subsection*{Loading Data from R
Packages}\label{loading-data-from-r-packages}

Many R packages include datasets that can be used for examples,
practice, and teaching. These datasets are useful because they can be
loaded in the same way on different computers, provided that the
required package has been installed. In this book, we use the
\textbf{liver} package, which provides curated datasets and utility
functions for data science examples and exercises.

One dataset used in several examples is \texttt{churn}, which contains
customer-level information for studying whether customers remain with a
company or discontinue their relationship. After installing the
\textbf{liver} package as described in Section
\ref{sec-R-install-packages}, the package and dataset can be loaded as
follows:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(liver)}

\FunctionTok{data}\NormalTok{(churn)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The command \texttt{library(liver)} makes the package available in the
current R session, while \texttt{data(churn)} loads the \texttt{churn}
dataset. Once loaded, \texttt{churn} can be used like any other data
frame in R and will also appear in the RStudio Environment panel. A
useful first step after loading any dataset is to examine its structure:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{str}\NormalTok{(churn)}
   \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}data.frame\textquotesingle{}}\SpecialCharTok{:}    \DecValTok{10127}\NormalTok{ obs. of  }\DecValTok{21}\NormalTok{ variables}\SpecialCharTok{:}
    \ErrorTok{$}\NormalTok{ customer\_ID          }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ int  }\DecValTok{768805383} \DecValTok{818770008} \DecValTok{713982108} \DecValTok{769911858} \DecValTok{709106358} \DecValTok{713061558} \DecValTok{810347208} \DecValTok{818906208} \DecValTok{710930508} \DecValTok{719661558}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ age                  }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ int  }\DecValTok{45} \DecValTok{49} \DecValTok{51} \DecValTok{40} \DecValTok{40} \DecValTok{44} \DecValTok{51} \DecValTok{32} \DecValTok{37} \DecValTok{48}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ gender               }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ Factor w}\SpecialCharTok{/} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{ levels }\StringTok{"female"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"male"}\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ education            }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ Factor w}\SpecialCharTok{/} \DecValTok{7}\NormalTok{ levels }\StringTok{"uneducated"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"highschool"}\NormalTok{,..}\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{4} \DecValTok{4} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{4} \DecValTok{7} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ marital              }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ Factor w}\SpecialCharTok{/} \DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{ levels }\StringTok{"married"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"single"}\NormalTok{,..}\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{4} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{4} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ income               }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ Factor w}\SpecialCharTok{/} \DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{ levels }\StringTok{"\textless{}40K"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"40K{-}60K"}\NormalTok{,..}\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{4} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{5} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ card\_category        }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ Factor w}\SpecialCharTok{/} \DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{ levels }\StringTok{"blue"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"silver"}\NormalTok{,..}\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ dependent\_count      }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ int  }\DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{5} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{4} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{4} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ months\_on\_book       }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ int  }\DecValTok{39} \DecValTok{44} \DecValTok{36} \DecValTok{34} \DecValTok{21} \DecValTok{36} \DecValTok{46} \DecValTok{27} \DecValTok{36} \DecValTok{36}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ relationship\_count   }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ int  }\DecValTok{5} \DecValTok{6} \DecValTok{4} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{5} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{6} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{5} \DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ months\_inactive      }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ int  }\DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{4} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ contacts\_count\_12    }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ int  }\DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{1} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{3} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ credit\_limit         }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ num  }\DecValTok{12691} \DecValTok{8256} \DecValTok{3418} \DecValTok{3313} \DecValTok{4716}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ revolving\_balance    }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ int  }\DecValTok{777} \DecValTok{864} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{2517} \DecValTok{0} \DecValTok{1247} \DecValTok{2264} \DecValTok{1396} \DecValTok{2517} \DecValTok{1677}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ available\_credit     }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ num  }\DecValTok{11914} \DecValTok{7392} \DecValTok{3418} \DecValTok{796} \DecValTok{4716}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ transaction\_amount\_12}\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ int  }\DecValTok{1144} \DecValTok{1291} \DecValTok{1887} \DecValTok{1171} \DecValTok{816} \DecValTok{1088} \DecValTok{1330} \DecValTok{1538} \DecValTok{1350} \DecValTok{1441}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ transaction\_count\_12 }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ int  }\DecValTok{42} \DecValTok{33} \DecValTok{20} \DecValTok{20} \DecValTok{28} \DecValTok{24} \DecValTok{31} \DecValTok{36} \DecValTok{24} \DecValTok{32}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ ratio\_amount\_Q4\_Q1   }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ num  }\FloatTok{1.33} \FloatTok{1.54} \FloatTok{2.59} \FloatTok{1.41} \FloatTok{2.17}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ ratio\_count\_Q4\_Q1    }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ num  }\FloatTok{1.62} \FloatTok{3.71} \FloatTok{2.33} \FloatTok{2.33} \FloatTok{2.5}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ utilization\_ratio    }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ num  }\FloatTok{0.061} \FloatTok{0.105} \DecValTok{0} \FloatTok{0.76} \DecValTok{0} \FloatTok{0.311} \FloatTok{0.066} \FloatTok{0.048} \FloatTok{0.113} \FloatTok{0.144}\NormalTok{ ...}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ churn                }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ Factor w}\SpecialCharTok{/} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{ levels }\StringTok{"yes"}\NormalTok{,}\StringTok{"no"}\SpecialCharTok{:} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{ ...}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Using datasets embedded in packages such as \textbf{liver} helps ensure
that examples can be rerun consistently across systems. The same dataset
can be loaded by readers, instructors, and collaborators without
manually downloading or locating external files.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Load the \texttt{churn} dataset from the \textbf{liver}
package and use \texttt{str(churn)} to inspect its variable structure.
Then use \texttt{head(churn)} to view the first few rows.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Importing Data with
RStudio}\label{importing-data-with-rstudio}

RStudio provides a graphical interface for importing data. This option
can be helpful when first learning R because it allows users to preview
a file and adjust import settings before loading the data. These
settings may include the file type, separator, column names, data types,
and character encoding.

To use this option, open the \emph{Environment} panel and select
\emph{Import Dataset} (see Figure \ref{fig-R-load-data}). RStudio then
prompts the user to choose the type of file to import. Text files,
including CSV and tab-delimited files, can be imported through the text
import options, while Excel files can be imported when the
\textbf{readxl} package is available.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{images/ch_R_RStudio-window-data-1.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-R-load-data}Using the `Import Dataset' option in
RStudio to load data.}

\end{figure}%

After a file is selected, RStudio displays a preview window where the
import settings can be checked and adjusted. Once the settings are
confirmed, the dataset is loaded into the R session and appears in the
RStudio Environment panel. This preview step is useful because it helps
detect common import problems, such as incorrect separators, missing
column names, or variables imported with unexpected data types.

The graphical interface is useful for exploration and for learning how
import options affect the resulting data frame. However, for
reproducible work, the code generated by RStudio should be copied into a
script or R Markdown document. This ensures that the import step can be
repeated without relying on manual clicks.

\subsection*{Importing CSV Files}\label{importing-csv-files}

In many projects, data are stored outside R in external files. One
common format is the comma-separated values file, or CSV file. A CSV
file is a plain-text file in which rows usually represent observations
and values within each row are separated by commas. CSV files are widely
used because they can be created and read by spreadsheet software,
databases, statistical programs, and many programming languages.

To import a CSV file using base R, use the \texttt{read.csv()} function:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{data }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{read.csv}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"path/to/your/file.csv"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The string \texttt{"path/to/your/file.csv"} should be replaced by the
actual file path. If the file is located in the current working
directory, only the file name is needed:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{data }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{read.csv}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"your\_file.csv"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The object \texttt{data} will contain the imported dataset as a data
frame. If the first row of the file does not contain column names, the
argument \texttt{header\ =\ FALSE} can be used:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{data }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{read.csv}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"your\_file.csv"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{header =} \ConstantTok{FALSE}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Files exported from spreadsheet software may occasionally contain
special characters or encoding marks. In such cases, specifying the file
encoding can help R interpret the file correctly:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{data }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{read.csv}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"your\_file.csv"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{fileEncoding =} \StringTok{"UTF{-}8{-}BOM"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

After importing a CSV file, it is good practice to inspect the resulting
data frame using functions such as \texttt{head()}, \texttt{str()}, and
\texttt{summary()}. These checks help confirm that the file has been
read correctly and that variables have the expected types.

\subsection*{Importing Excel Files}\label{importing-excel-files}

Excel files are also common in business, education, and research
settings. To import \texttt{.xlsx} or \texttt{.xls} files into R, the
\textbf{readxl} package provides the \texttt{read\_excel()} function. If
the package has not yet been installed, it can be installed using the
methods described in Section \ref{sec-R-install-packages}.

Once \textbf{readxl} is installed, an Excel file can be imported as
follows:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(readxl)}

\NormalTok{data }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{read\_excel}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"path/to/your/file.xlsx"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The file path should be replaced with the location of the Excel file on
your system. The imported object can then be inspected using functions
such as \texttt{head()}, \texttt{str()}, and \texttt{summary()}, as with
other tabular datasets in R.

If the workbook contains multiple sheets, the \texttt{sheet} argument
can be used to select a specific sheet by name or by position:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{data }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{read\_excel}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"path/to/your/file.xlsx"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{sheet =} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Excel workbooks sometimes contain merged cells, notes above the table,
multiple header rows, or several tables on the same sheet. These
features can make import more difficult because they obscure the
rectangular structure expected by most data analysis tools. For
reproducible analysis, it is usually better to work with files that
contain a single table, one row of column names, and one row per
observation.

\subsection*{Working Directories and Relative
Paths}\label{working-directories-and-relative-paths}

When importing data from external files, R needs to know where the file
is located. The \emph{working directory} is the folder that R uses as
its default location for reading input files and saving output. To check
the current working directory, use:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{getwd}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If a file cannot be found, checking the working directory is often a
useful first diagnostic step. The working directory can be changed
through the RStudio menu or by using \texttt{setwd()}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{setwd}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"\textasciitilde{}/Documents"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The \texttt{setwd()} function can be useful during interactive work, but
repeatedly changing the working directory inside scripts can make an
analysis less reproducible. A path that works on one computer may fail
on another. For this reason, it is usually better to organize analyses
inside an RStudio Project and use relative file paths. An RStudio
Project treats the project folder as the starting point for the
analysis, making it easier to keep scripts, data, figures, and reports
together.

For example, if a project contains a folder called \texttt{data}, a CSV
file inside that folder can be imported using a relative path:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{data }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{read.csv}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"data/your\_file.csv"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This approach is more portable than hard-coding a full path to a folder
on one specific computer. Establishing a clear project structure early
makes later analyses easier to rerun, share, and document.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Use \texttt{getwd()} to display the current working
directory. Then create or open an RStudio Project, create a folder
called \texttt{data}, and consider how a file inside that folder could
be imported using a relative path such as
\texttt{"data/your\_file.csv"}.
\end{quote}

\section{Data Types in R}\label{data-types-in-r}

In R, every object has a data type. Data types determine how values are
stored and how functions interpret them. Recognizing the correct type is
important because many operations behave differently depending on
whether a value is numeric, textual, logical, or categorical.

Table \ref{tbl-R-data-types} summarizes common data types encountered in
data analysis with R. These types often appear together in real
datasets. For example, a customer dataset may contain numeric variables
such as income, character variables such as customer names, logical
variables indicating whether a condition is true, and factor variables
representing categories such as churn status.

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1528}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3611}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.4861}}@{}}
\caption{Common data types in R and their typical
uses.}\label{tbl-R-data-types}\tabularnewline
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Type
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Example
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Typical use
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endfirsthead
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Type
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Example
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Typical use
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
numeric & \texttt{3.14} & Continuous measurements \\
integer & \texttt{42L} & Counts and indices \\
character & \texttt{"yes"} & Text values and labels \\
logical & \texttt{TRUE} & Conditions and comparisons \\
factor & \texttt{factor(c("yes",\ "no"))} & Categorical variables with
levels \\
\end{longtable}

Numeric values are used for real numbers, such as prices, measurements,
or model predictions. Integer values represent whole numbers and are
created explicitly in R by adding \texttt{L}, as in \texttt{42L};
otherwise, whole numbers are usually stored as numeric values. Character
values store text, while logical values take the form \texttt{TRUE} or
\texttt{FALSE} and often arise from comparisons. Factors represent
categorical variables with a fixed set of levels. They are especially
important in modeling and grouped visualizations because many R
functions treat factors differently from ordinary character variables.

In this chapter, the focus is on how R represents values internally
through data types. The broader statistical distinction between feature
types, such as continuous and categorical variables, is introduced in
Section \ref{sec-eda-feature-types}. The two ideas are related but not
identical: data types describe how R stores values, while feature types
describe how variables should be understood in an analysis.

To check the type or class of an object, use functions such as
\texttt{class()}, \texttt{typeof()}, and \texttt{str()}. The function
\texttt{class()} reports the broad class that R assigns to an object,
\texttt{typeof()} describes its internal storage mode, and
\texttt{str()} gives a compact overview of more complex objects such as
data frames:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{class}\NormalTok{(prices)}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\StringTok{"numeric"}

\FunctionTok{typeof}\NormalTok{(prices)}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\StringTok{"double"}

\FunctionTok{str}\NormalTok{(prices)}
\NormalTok{    num [}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{] }\DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{37} \DecValTok{61}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The importance of data types becomes clear when a variable is stored in
an unsuitable form. For example, the following vector contains numbers
written inside quotation marks, so R treats them as character values
rather than numeric values:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{income }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"42000"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"28000"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"60000"}\NormalTok{)}

\FunctionTok{mean}\NormalTok{(income)}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\ConstantTok{NA}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Because \texttt{income} is stored as text, \texttt{mean()} cannot
compute the average in the intended way. The values must first be
converted to numeric form:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{income }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{as.numeric}\NormalTok{(income)}

\FunctionTok{mean}\NormalTok{(income)}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\FloatTok{43333.33}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Chapter \ref{sec-chapter-data-understanding} explains why data types
matter when summarizing, visualizing, and interpreting variables during
data exploration. For now, the main lesson is that inspecting data types
is an essential first step when working with any dataset.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Load the \texttt{churn} dataset from the \textbf{liver}
package, as introduced in Section \ref{sec-R-import-data}. Use
\texttt{str(churn)} to inspect its structure. Which variables are
numeric, character, logical, or factors? Then apply \texttt{class()} and
\texttt{typeof()} to a few columns to examine how R represents them
internally.
\end{quote}

\section{Data Structures in R}\label{data-structures-in-r}

Data structures determine how values are organized and stored in R.
While data types describe \emph{what kind} of values an object contains,
such as numeric, character, or logical values, data structures describe
\emph{how} those values are arranged. A single value, a sequence of
values, a rectangular table, and a collection of different objects
require different structures.

The most common data structures in R include vectors, matrices, data
frames, lists, and arrays. Vectors store one-dimensional sequences of
values of the same type. Matrices store two-dimensional rectangular
collections of values of the same type. Data frames store tabular data
in rows and columns, where different columns may have different types.
Lists can combine several objects of different types and sizes. Arrays
extend matrices to more than two dimensions, but they are less central
in the examples in this book. Figure \ref{fig-R-objects} provides a
visual overview of these core structures.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.65\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{images/ch_R_R-objects.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-R-objects}A visual guide to common data structures
in R, organized by dimensionality and type uniformity.}

\end{figure}%

In this section, we focus on vectors, matrices, data frames, and lists.
The emphasis is on recognizing these structures and understanding when
they are used. In the rest of the book, most datasets are represented as
data frames, so this structure receives particular attention.

\subsection*{Vectors in R}\label{vectors-in-r}

A \emph{vector} is the most basic data structure in R. It stores a
one-dimensional sequence of values, all of the same type. For example, a
vector may contain only numbers, only character strings, or only logical
values. Vectors are important because many other data structures,
including matrices and data frames, are built from them.

A vector can be created using the \texttt{c()} function, which combines
values into a single object:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{prices }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{37}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{61}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{prices}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]  }\DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{37} \DecValTok{61}

\FunctionTok{length}\NormalTok{(prices)}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\DecValTok{3}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In this example, \texttt{prices} is a numeric vector containing three
values. The function \texttt{length()} returns the number of elements in
the vector. Since all elements of a vector must have the same type, R
may convert values automatically if different types are mixed. For
example:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{mixed\_values }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"a"}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{mixed\_values}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\StringTok{"1"} \StringTok{"a"} \StringTok{"3"}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Here, the numeric values are converted to character values because the
vector must store all elements using a common type. This automatic
conversion is called \emph{coercion} and is useful to recognize when
inspecting data.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Create a numeric vector with at least four values and
use \texttt{length()} to check how many elements it contains. Then
create a second vector that mixes numbers and text, such as
\texttt{c(1,\ "a",\ 3)}, and observe how R represents the result.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Matrices in R}\label{matrices-in-r}

A \emph{matrix} is a two-dimensional data structure with rows and
columns. Like a vector, a matrix stores values of a single type.
Matrices are common in mathematics, statistics, and machine learning,
especially when working with numerical operations.

A matrix can be created using the \texttt{matrix()} function:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{my\_matrix }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{matrix}\NormalTok{(}\FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{), }\AttributeTok{nrow =} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{ncol =} \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{byrow =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{my\_matrix}
\NormalTok{        [,}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] [,}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{] [,}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,]    }\DecValTok{1}    \DecValTok{2}    \DecValTok{3}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{,]    }\DecValTok{4}    \DecValTok{5}    \DecValTok{6}

\FunctionTok{dim}\NormalTok{(my\_matrix)}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{3}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This creates a \(2 \times 3\) matrix filled row by row. The function
\texttt{dim()} returns the number of rows and columns. Individual
elements can be accessed using row and column indices:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{my\_matrix[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\DecValTok{2}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Matrices are useful for numerical computations, but they are less
flexible than data frames because every element must have the same type.
For most tabular datasets in this book, data frames are therefore more
appropriate.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Create a \(3 \times 3\) matrix with your own numbers.
Use \texttt{dim()} to check its size and retrieve the value in the third
row and first column.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Data Frames in R}\label{data-frames-in-r}

A \emph{data frame} is the main structure used for tabular data in R. It
organizes data into rows and columns, where each row typically
represents an observation and each column represents a variable. Unlike
matrices, data frames allow different columns to have different data
types. For example, one column may contain numeric values, another may
contain character labels, and another may contain logical or factor
values.

This flexibility makes data frames central to data science with R.
Datasets imported from CSV or Excel files are usually stored as data
frames, and many datasets provided by R packages also use this
structure. Most examples, case studies, and exercises in this book
therefore involve data frames.

A data frame can be created by combining vectors of equal length:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{student\_id }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{101}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{102}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{103}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{104}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{name }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Mahsa"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Alex"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Emma"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Rob"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{age }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{22}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{21}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{19}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{grade }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"A"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"B"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"A"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"C"}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{students\_df }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{data.frame}\NormalTok{(student\_id, name, age, grade)}

\NormalTok{students\_df}
\NormalTok{     student\_id  name age grade}
   \DecValTok{1}        \DecValTok{101}\NormalTok{ Mahsa  }\DecValTok{22}\NormalTok{     A}
   \DecValTok{2}        \DecValTok{102}\NormalTok{  Alex  }\DecValTok{21}\NormalTok{     B}
   \DecValTok{3}        \DecValTok{103}\NormalTok{  Emma  }\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{     A}
   \DecValTok{4}        \DecValTok{104}\NormalTok{   Rob  }\DecValTok{19}\NormalTok{     C}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This creates a data frame named \texttt{students\_df} with four rows and
four columns. Its class and structure can be inspected using:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{class}\NormalTok{(students\_df)}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\StringTok{"data.frame"}

\FunctionTok{str}\NormalTok{(students\_df)}
   \StringTok{\textquotesingle{}data.frame\textquotesingle{}}\SpecialCharTok{:}    \DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{ obs. of  }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{ variables}\SpecialCharTok{:}
    \ErrorTok{$}\NormalTok{ student\_id}\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ num  }\DecValTok{101} \DecValTok{102} \DecValTok{103} \DecValTok{104}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ name      }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ chr  }\StringTok{"Mahsa"} \StringTok{"Alex"} \StringTok{"Emma"} \StringTok{"Rob"}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ age       }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ num  }\DecValTok{22} \DecValTok{21} \DecValTok{20} \DecValTok{19}
    \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{ grade     }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{ chr  }\StringTok{"A"} \StringTok{"B"} \StringTok{"A"} \StringTok{"C"}

\FunctionTok{summary}\NormalTok{(students\_df)}
\NormalTok{      student\_id        name                age           grade          }
\NormalTok{    Min.   }\SpecialCharTok{:}\FloatTok{101.0}\NormalTok{   Length}\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{           Min.   }\SpecialCharTok{:}\FloatTok{19.00}\NormalTok{   Length}\SpecialCharTok{:}\DecValTok{4}          
    \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{st Qu.}\SpecialCharTok{:}\FloatTok{101.8}\NormalTok{   Class }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{character   }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{st Qu.}\SpecialCharTok{:}\FloatTok{19.75}\NormalTok{   Class }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{character  }
\NormalTok{    Median }\SpecialCharTok{:}\FloatTok{102.5}\NormalTok{   Mode  }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{character   Median }\SpecialCharTok{:}\FloatTok{20.50}\NormalTok{   Mode  }\SpecialCharTok{:}\NormalTok{character  }
\NormalTok{    Mean   }\SpecialCharTok{:}\FloatTok{102.5}\NormalTok{                      Mean   }\SpecialCharTok{:}\FloatTok{20.50}                     
    \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{rd Qu.}\SpecialCharTok{:}\FloatTok{103.2}                      \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{rd Qu.}\SpecialCharTok{:}\FloatTok{21.25}                     
\NormalTok{    Max.   }\SpecialCharTok{:}\FloatTok{104.0}\NormalTok{                      Max.   }\SpecialCharTok{:}\FloatTok{22.00}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The function \texttt{class()} confirms that \texttt{students\_df} is a
data frame, \texttt{str()} provides a compact overview of its columns
and data types, and \texttt{summary()} provides basic summaries for each
column. These functions are useful when inspecting a newly created or
loaded dataset.

Individual columns can be accessed using the \texttt{\$} operator:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{students\_df}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{age}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\DecValTok{22} \DecValTok{21} \DecValTok{20} \DecValTok{19}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Columns can also be modified or added. For example, the following code
creates a new logical column indicating whether each student is at least
21 years old:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{students\_df}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{is\_adult }\OtherTok{=}\NormalTok{ students\_df}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{age }\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}=} \DecValTok{21}

\NormalTok{students\_df}
\NormalTok{     student\_id  name age grade is\_adult}
   \DecValTok{1}        \DecValTok{101}\NormalTok{ Mahsa  }\DecValTok{22}\NormalTok{     A     }\ConstantTok{TRUE}
   \DecValTok{2}        \DecValTok{102}\NormalTok{  Alex  }\DecValTok{21}\NormalTok{     B     }\ConstantTok{TRUE}
   \DecValTok{3}        \DecValTok{103}\NormalTok{  Emma  }\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{     A    }\ConstantTok{FALSE}
   \DecValTok{4}        \DecValTok{104}\NormalTok{   Rob  }\DecValTok{19}\NormalTok{     C    }\ConstantTok{FALSE}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Data frames are especially useful in real-world analysis because
datasets often mix numerical and categorical variables. The
\texttt{churn} dataset introduced in Section \ref{sec-R-import-data},
for example, is stored as a data frame and contains variables of several
types. This is typical of the datasets used throughout the book:
observations are arranged in rows, variables are arranged in columns,
and different columns may represent different kinds of information.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Create a small data frame with three columns: one
numeric, one character, and one logical. Use \texttt{class()},
\texttt{str()}, and \texttt{summary()} to inspect it. Then add a new
column using a logical condition.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Lists in R}\label{lists-in-r}

A \emph{list} is a flexible data structure that can store objects of
different types and sizes. A list may contain vectors, matrices, data
frames, model outputs, or even other lists. Lists are useful when
several related objects need to be stored together.

The following example creates a list containing the vector, matrix, and
data frame introduced above:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{my\_list }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{prices =}\NormalTok{ prices, }\AttributeTok{matrix =}\NormalTok{ my\_matrix, }\AttributeTok{students =}\NormalTok{ students\_df)}

\NormalTok{my\_list}
   \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{prices}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]  }\DecValTok{2} \DecValTok{37} \DecValTok{61}
   
   \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{matrix}
\NormalTok{        [,}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] [,}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{] [,}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,]    }\DecValTok{1}    \DecValTok{2}    \DecValTok{3}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{,]    }\DecValTok{4}    \DecValTok{5}    \DecValTok{6}
   
   \SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{students}
\NormalTok{     student\_id  name age grade is\_adult}
   \DecValTok{1}        \DecValTok{101}\NormalTok{ Mahsa  }\DecValTok{22}\NormalTok{     A     }\ConstantTok{TRUE}
   \DecValTok{2}        \DecValTok{102}\NormalTok{  Alex  }\DecValTok{21}\NormalTok{     B     }\ConstantTok{TRUE}
   \DecValTok{3}        \DecValTok{103}\NormalTok{  Emma  }\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{     A    }\ConstantTok{FALSE}
   \DecValTok{4}        \DecValTok{104}\NormalTok{   Rob  }\DecValTok{19}\NormalTok{     C    }\ConstantTok{FALSE}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Individual components of a list can be accessed using their names or
their positions:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{my\_list}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{students}
\NormalTok{     student\_id  name age grade is\_adult}
   \DecValTok{1}        \DecValTok{101}\NormalTok{ Mahsa  }\DecValTok{22}\NormalTok{     A     }\ConstantTok{TRUE}
   \DecValTok{2}        \DecValTok{102}\NormalTok{  Alex  }\DecValTok{21}\NormalTok{     B     }\ConstantTok{TRUE}
   \DecValTok{3}        \DecValTok{103}\NormalTok{  Emma  }\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{     A    }\ConstantTok{FALSE}
   \DecValTok{4}        \DecValTok{104}\NormalTok{   Rob  }\DecValTok{19}\NormalTok{     C    }\ConstantTok{FALSE}

\NormalTok{my\_list[[}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{]]}
\NormalTok{        [,}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] [,}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{] [,}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{,]    }\DecValTok{1}    \DecValTok{2}    \DecValTok{3}
\NormalTok{   [}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{,]    }\DecValTok{4}    \DecValTok{5}    \DecValTok{6}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Lists appear frequently in R because many modeling functions return
results as lists. For example, a fitted model may store coefficients,
residuals, fitted values, and diagnostic information inside a single
object. At this stage, it is enough to recognize that lists are
containers for related objects that do not all need to have the same
structure.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Create a list containing a character vector, a logical
vector, and a small data frame. Access each component using \texttt{\$}
or double square brackets.
\end{quote}

\section{How to Merge Data in R}\label{sec-R-merge-data}

In real-world data analysis, information is often stored across multiple
tables rather than in one complete dataset. For example, customer
characteristics may be stored in one table, while transaction records
are stored in another. Merging datasets allows related information to be
combined into a single data frame so that it can be explored,
visualized, or modeled together.

Merging relies on the concept of a \emph{key}: a column that identifies
which rows in one table correspond to rows in another. In base R, the
\texttt{merge()} function joins two data frames using one or more shared
key columns:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{merge}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ data\_frame1, }\AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ data\_frame2, }\AttributeTok{by =} \StringTok{"column\_name"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Consider two small data frames. The first contains customer information,
while the second contains purchase information. Both include an
\texttt{id} column, which can be used as the key:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{customers }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{data.frame}\NormalTok{(}
  \AttributeTok{id =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{),}
  \AttributeTok{name =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Mahsa"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Eva"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Alex"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Jack"}\NormalTok{),}
  \AttributeTok{age =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{22}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{28}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{35}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{purchases }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{data.frame}\NormalTok{(}
  \AttributeTok{id =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{),}
  \AttributeTok{amount =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{50}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{60}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{70}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{80}\NormalTok{),}
  \AttributeTok{product =} \FunctionTok{c}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"book"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"laptop"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"phone"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"tablet"}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

An \emph{inner join} keeps only rows with matching key values in both
data frames. In base R, this is the default behavior of
\texttt{merge()}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{merged\_inner }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{merge}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ customers, }\AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ purchases, }\AttributeTok{by =} \StringTok{"id"}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{merged\_inner}
\NormalTok{     id name age amount product}
   \DecValTok{1}  \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{ Alex  }\DecValTok{35}     \DecValTok{50}\NormalTok{    book}
   \DecValTok{2}  \DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{ Jack  }\DecValTok{20}     \DecValTok{60}\NormalTok{  laptop}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In this example, only customers with \texttt{id} values appearing in
both \texttt{customers} and \texttt{purchases} are retained. A
\emph{left join} keeps all rows from the first data frame and adds
matching information from the second data frame when available. This is
done by setting \texttt{all.x\ =\ TRUE}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{merged\_left }\OtherTok{=} \FunctionTok{merge}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ customers, }\AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ purchases, }\AttributeTok{by =} \StringTok{"id"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{all.x =} \ConstantTok{TRUE}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{merged\_left}
\NormalTok{     id  name age amount product}
   \DecValTok{1}  \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{ Mahsa  }\DecValTok{22}     \ConstantTok{NA}    \SpecialCharTok{\textless{}}\ConstantTok{NA}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}}
   \DecValTok{2}  \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{   Eva  }\DecValTok{28}     \ConstantTok{NA}    \SpecialCharTok{\textless{}}\ConstantTok{NA}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}}
   \DecValTok{3}  \DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{  Alex  }\DecValTok{35}     \DecValTok{50}\NormalTok{    book}
   \DecValTok{4}  \DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{  Jack  }\DecValTok{20}     \DecValTok{60}\NormalTok{  laptop}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Rows without a match in the second data frame receive \texttt{NA} values
in the added columns. Other join types are also possible. Setting
\texttt{all.y\ =\ TRUE} performs a right join, while setting
\texttt{all\ =\ TRUE} performs a full join. Figure \ref{fig-R-merging}
summarizes these common join types visually.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.75\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{images/ch_R_merging.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-R-merging}Illustration of inner, left, right, and
full joins, showing how rows are retained or discarded based on shared
key values.}

\end{figure}%

After merging data, it is good practice to check the number of rows and
inspect the result. Unexpected row counts or many missing values may
indicate mismatched keys, duplicate identifiers, or incompatible column
types.

\section{Data Visualization in R}\label{sec-R-visualization}

Data visualization plays a central role in data science because it helps
transform raw values into visual patterns. Visual summaries can reveal
trends, unusual observations, group differences, and relationships
between variables that may be difficult to detect from numerical
summaries alone. In Chapter \ref{sec-chapter-data-understanding},
visualization plays an important role in Data Understanding and
Exploration. In this chapter, we begin with a first example using
\textbf{ggplot2}.

The \textbf{ggplot2} package is one of the main visualization tools used
in this book. At its core, a \textbf{ggplot2} visualization combines
three essential components: the dataset to be visualized, the aesthetic
mappings that connect variables to visual properties such as position or
color, and the geometric object, or \emph{geom}, that determines how the
data are displayed. For example, a scatter plot uses points to show the
relationship between two numerical variables.

These components provide the foundation for building plots in
\textbf{ggplot2}. More advanced visualizations may also include
additional layers that control facets, statistical transformations,
coordinate systems, and themes. Together, these elements form the
grammar underlying \textbf{ggplot2} visualizations. Figure
\ref{fig-R-ggplot-layers} provides a visual overview of these layers. In
this chapter, we focus mainly on the first three components: data,
aesthetics, and geoms. The remaining layers are introduced gradually
throughout the book when they become useful for exploratory analysis and
communication.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{images/ch_R_ggplot_layers.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-R-ggplot-layers}Main layers of a ggplot2
visualization. In this chapter, the emphasis is on data, aesthetics, and
geoms; additional layers are introduced throughout the book.}

\end{figure}%

Before using \textbf{ggplot2}, install the package as described in
Section \ref{sec-R-install-packages}, and then load it into the current
R session:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{library}\NormalTok{(ggplot2)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To create a simple scatter plot using the \texttt{churn} dataset, we
first specify the dataset and then map two numerical variables to the
horizontal and vertical axes. The variables
\texttt{transaction\_amount\_12} and \texttt{transaction\_count\_12}
summarize customer transaction activity over a 12-month period:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ churn, }
       \AttributeTok{mapping =} \FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ transaction\_amount\_12, }\AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ transaction\_count\_12)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_point}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.65\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{Appendix-r-foundations_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-46-1.pdf}
\end{center}

In this example, \texttt{ggplot()} starts the plot, \texttt{aes()}
defines how variables are mapped to visual features, and
\texttt{geom\_point()} adds the points. Each point represents one
observation in the dataset. The resulting plot provides an initial view
of the relationship between transaction amount and transaction count.

A common template for \textbf{ggplot2} visualizations is:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{data =} \SpecialCharTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{DATA}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{mapping =} \FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialCharTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{MAPPINGS}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}}\NormalTok{)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \ErrorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{GEOM\_FUNCTION}\SpecialCharTok{\textgreater{}}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The placeholders are replaced by the dataset, the variables to be shown,
and the type of plot to be created. This structure is used repeatedly
throughout the book, with different datasets and different geometric
functions. The next subsections introduce two important parts of this
structure in more detail: geom functions, which determine the type of
plot, and aesthetics, which specify how variables are mapped to visual
features.

\subsection*{Geom Functions in ggplot2}\label{geom-functions-in-ggplot2}

In \textbf{ggplot2}, \emph{geom functions} determine how data are
represented visually. Each function whose name begins with
\texttt{geom\_} adds a geometric object to a plot. The dataset and
aesthetic mappings describe \emph{what} is shown, while the geom
specifies \emph{how} the data appear.

The previous example used \texttt{geom\_point()} to create a scatter
plot, which is useful for examining the relationship between two
numerical variables. Two other geom functions are especially useful at
this stage: \texttt{geom\_histogram()} and \texttt{geom\_boxplot()}. A
histogram shows the distribution of a single numerical variable, while a
boxplot summarizes the distribution of a numerical variable and is
useful for comparing groups.

To examine the distribution of one numerical variable, we can use
\texttt{geom\_histogram()}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ churn, }\AttributeTok{mapping =} \FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ transaction\_amount\_12)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_histogram}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.65\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{Appendix-r-foundations_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-48-1.pdf}
\end{center}

To compare a numerical variable across groups, we can use
\texttt{geom\_boxplot()}. For example, the following plot compares
12-month transaction amounts for customers who churned and those who did
not:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ churn, }\AttributeTok{mapping =} \FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ churn, }\AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ transaction\_amount\_12)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_boxplot}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.65\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{Appendix-r-foundations_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-49-1.pdf}
\end{center}

Together, these three geoms provide a useful starting point for visual
exploration: scatter plots for relationships, histograms for
distributions, and boxplots for group comparisons. More advanced plot
types and additional \textbf{ggplot2} layers are introduced in Chapter
\ref{sec-chapter-data-understanding}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Using the \texttt{churn} dataset, create a histogram
with \texttt{geom\_histogram()} and a boxplot with
\texttt{geom\_boxplot()}. Then return to the scatter plot from the
previous example and describe what type of question each visualization
helps answer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Aesthetics in ggplot2}\label{aesthetics-in-ggplot2}

In \textbf{ggplot2}, aesthetics control how variables are represented
visually. Common aesthetics include position, color, size, shape, and
transparency. In this chapter, the most important idea is the
distinction between \emph{mapping} an aesthetic to a variable and
\emph{setting} an aesthetic to a fixed value.

When an aesthetic is placed inside \texttt{aes()}, it is mapped to a
variable in the data. For example, the following plot maps color to the
\texttt{churn} variable, so customers who churned and those who did not
are shown using different colors:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ churn, }\AttributeTok{mapping =} \FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ transaction\_amount\_12, }\AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ transaction\_count\_12, }\AttributeTok{color =}\NormalTok{ churn)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_point}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.65\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{Appendix-r-foundations_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-50-1.pdf}
\end{center}

Because \texttt{color\ =\ churn} is specified inside \texttt{aes()}, the
color of each point depends on the value of the \texttt{churn} variable.
\textbf{ggplot2} also creates a legend automatically, since the color
now carries information about the data.

By contrast, when aesthetics are set outside \texttt{aes()}, they are
treated as fixed visual settings. In the following plot, all points are
displayed using the same color and point size:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\FunctionTok{ggplot}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{data =}\NormalTok{ churn, }\AttributeTok{mapping =} \FunctionTok{aes}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{x =}\NormalTok{ transaction\_amount\_12, }\AttributeTok{y =}\NormalTok{ transaction\_count\_12)) }\SpecialCharTok{+}
  \FunctionTok{geom\_point}\NormalTok{(}\AttributeTok{color =} \StringTok{"\#1B3B6F"}\NormalTok{, }\AttributeTok{size =} \FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.65\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{Appendix-r-foundations_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-51-1.pdf}
\end{center}

In this case, color and size are not linked to variables in the dataset,
so no legend is created for them. This distinction is important: use
\texttt{aes()} when a visual feature should represent information from
the data, and place the setting outside \texttt{aes()} when the feature
should be the same for all observations.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Using the \texttt{churn} dataset, create a scatter plot
of \texttt{ratio\_amount\_Q4\_Q1} versus \texttt{ratio\_count\_Q4\_Q1}.
First, map color to the \texttt{churn} variable inside \texttt{aes()}.
Then create a second version in which all points have the same fixed
color outside \texttt{aes()}. Compare the two plots.
\end{quote}

Together, \texttt{ggplot()}, \texttt{aes()}, and a small number of geom
functions provide a practical starting point for data visualization in
R. Chapter \ref{sec-chapter-data-understanding} extends this foundation
by discussing how to choose appropriate plot types, refine graphics, and
interpret visual patterns as part of exploratory data analysis.

\section{Formulas in R}\label{sec-R-formula-in-R}

Many modeling functions in R use \emph{formulas} to describe
relationships between variables. A formula uses the tilde symbol
\texttt{\textasciitilde{}} to separate the response variable from the
predictor variables. The basic structure is:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{response }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ predictor1 }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ predictor2 }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ ...}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The variable on the left-hand side is the outcome to be explained or
predicted, while the variables on the right-hand side are the
predictors. For example, a model for diamond price using carat, cut, and
color as predictors could be written as:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{price }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ carat }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ cut }\SpecialCharTok{+}\NormalTok{ color}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The formula does not perform the calculation by itself. Instead, it
tells a modeling function which variables should be used and how they
are related in the model specification. A common shorthand is the dot
notation:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{price }\SpecialCharTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{ .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Here, the dot represents all remaining variables in the dataset as
predictors. This notation can be useful, but it should be used carefully
because it may include variables that are not appropriate for a
particular analysis.

Formulas are introduced here only as notation. They are used throughout
the book for classification and regression models, where their meaning
and role in model fitting are explained in more detail.

\section{Reporting with R Markdown}\label{sec-R-rmarkdown}

How can an analysis be shared in a way that combines code, results, and
explanation in a single coherent document? This question is central to
reproducible data science. In many analyses, the code used to produce a
result is stored separately from the written explanation, which can make
it difficult to check, update, or reproduce the work. R Markdown
addresses this problem by allowing narrative text, executable R code,
tables, and figures to be combined in one document.

Clear reporting is an important part of the Data Science Workflow.
Analyses that are statistically sound and computationally careful have
limited value if their results are not communicated clearly. Whether the
audience consists of technical collaborators, students, managers, or
policy makers, an effective report should explain not only what was
found, but also how the results were obtained.

R Markdown supports this goal by creating documents that can be rendered
into formats such as HTML, PDF, and Word. Files written in the
\texttt{.Rmd} format provide an executable record of an analysis: when
the document is rendered, the code is run and the output is inserted
into the report. The subsections below introduce the basic structure of
an R Markdown document, beginning with the YAML header and then moving
to code chunks, inline code, and simple text formatting.

\subsection*{Creating an R Markdown
Document}\label{creating-an-r-markdown-document}

R Markdown separates writing from rendering. The source file is written
in plain text and contains narrative, code chunks, and formatting
instructions. When the document is rendered, R executes the code chunks,
generates the output, and inserts results such as tables and figures
into the final report. This workflow helps keep the explanation, code,
and results synchronized when the analysis changes.

To create a new R Markdown file in RStudio, select:

\begin{quote}
\emph{File \textgreater{} New File \textgreater{} R Markdown}
\end{quote}

A dialog box then appears where the title, author name, and output
format can be specified. For most introductory analyses and assignments,
the ``Document'' option is appropriate. HTML is often a convenient first
output format because it renders quickly and provides clear feedback
during development. PDF and Word output can be used later when a
different format is required.

R Markdown files use the \texttt{.Rmd} extension, which distinguishes
them from standard R scripts with the \texttt{.R} extension. A new
\texttt{.Rmd} file usually opens with a built-in template that contains
example text, code chunks, and formatting. This template can be rendered
immediately and then modified step by step as the structure of the
document becomes clearer.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Create a new R Markdown file in RStudio and render it
without making any changes. Then modify the title, add a short sentence
of your own, and render the document again. Observe how the output
changes when the source file is updated.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The YAML Header}\label{the-yaml-header}

At the top of every R Markdown file is a section called the \emph{YAML
header}. This header contains metadata that controls how the document is
rendered, including the title, author, date, and output format. It is
enclosed between three dashes (\texttt{-\/-\/-}) at the beginning of the
file.

A simple YAML header may look as follows:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\PreprocessorTok{{-}{-}{-}}
\FunctionTok{title}\KeywordTok{:}\AttributeTok{ }\StringTok{"Exploring a Dataset with R"}
\FunctionTok{author}\KeywordTok{:}\AttributeTok{ }\StringTok{"Your Name"}
\FunctionTok{date}\KeywordTok{:}\AttributeTok{ }\StringTok{"Today\textquotesingle{}s Date"}
\FunctionTok{output}\KeywordTok{:}\AttributeTok{ html\_document}
\PreprocessorTok{{-}{-}{-}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In this example, \texttt{title} sets the title displayed at the top of
the report, \texttt{author} identifies the person who prepared the
document, \texttt{date} records the date of the report, and
\texttt{output} specifies the format to be produced. The value
\texttt{html\_document} creates an HTML file, while other common options
include \texttt{pdf\_document} and \texttt{word\_document}.

The YAML header can also include additional options. For example, a
table of contents can be added to an HTML report by writing:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\PreprocessorTok{{-}{-}{-}}
\FunctionTok{title}\KeywordTok{:}\AttributeTok{ }\StringTok{"Exploring a Dataset with R"}
\FunctionTok{author}\KeywordTok{:}\AttributeTok{ }\StringTok{"Your Name"}
\FunctionTok{date}\KeywordTok{:}\AttributeTok{ }\StringTok{"Today\textquotesingle{}s Date"}
\FunctionTok{output}\KeywordTok{:}
\AttributeTok{  }\FunctionTok{html\_document}\KeywordTok{:}
\AttributeTok{    }\FunctionTok{toc}\KeywordTok{:}\AttributeTok{ }\CharTok{true}
\PreprocessorTok{{-}{-}{-}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This option is useful for longer reports with several sections. Since
YAML is sensitive to indentation, the spacing should be written
carefully, especially when options are nested under an output format.
For most introductory reports, however, a simple header with a title,
author, date, and output format is sufficient.

\subsection*{Code Chunks and Inline
Code}\label{code-chunks-and-inline-code}

One of the defining features of R Markdown is its ability to combine
code and narrative in the same document. This is done through \emph{code
chunks} and \emph{inline code}. Code chunks are used for longer pieces
of R code, such as loading data, creating summaries, fitting models, or
producing figures. Inline code is used for short expressions that should
appear directly within a sentence.

A code chunk is a block of code enclosed in triple backticks
(\texttt{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}}) and
marked with a chunk header that specifies the language (in this case,
\texttt{\{r\}}). For example:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\InformationTok{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\{r\}}
\InformationTok{2 + 3}
\InformationTok{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
   [1] 5
\end{verbatim}

When the document is rendered, R executes the code and inserts the
output at the appropriate location. Code chunks are commonly used for
data wrangling, statistical modeling, creating visualizations, and
running simulations. To run individual chunks interactively in RStudio,
click the \emph{Run} button at the top of the chunk or press
\texttt{Ctrl\ +\ Shift\ +\ Enter}. See Figure \ref{fig-R-run-chunk} for
a visual reference.

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{images/ch_R_run-chunk.png}

}

\caption{\label{fig-R-run-chunk}R Markdown example with executing a code
chunk in R Markdown using the `Run' button in RStudio.}

\end{figure}%

Code chunks support a variety of options that control how code and
output are displayed. These options are specified in the chunk header.
Table \ref{tbl-R-chunk-options} summarizes how these options affect what
appears in the final report. For example:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{echo\ =\ FALSE} hides the code but still displays the output.
\item
  \texttt{eval\ =\ FALSE} shows the code but does not execute it.
\item
  \texttt{message\ =\ FALSE} suppresses messages generated by functions
  (e.g., when loading packages).
\item
  \texttt{warning\ =\ FALSE} hides warning messages.
\item
  \texttt{error\ =\ FALSE} stops rendering when an error occurs.
\item
  \texttt{include\ =\ FALSE} runs the code but omits both the code and
  its output.
\end{itemize}

\begin{table}

\caption{\label{tbl-R-chunk-options}Behavior of code chunk options and
their impact on execution, visibility, and outputs.}

\centering{

\centering
\resizebox{\ifdim\width>\linewidth\linewidth\else\width\fi}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{cccccccc}
\toprule
Option & Run Code & Show Code & Output & Plots & Messages & Warnings & Errors\\
\midrule
\texttt{echo = FALSE} & $\checkmark$ & $\times$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$\\
\texttt{eval = FALSE} & $\times$ & $\checkmark$ & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$\\
\texttt{message = FALSE} & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\times$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$\\
\texttt{warning = FALSE} & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\times$ & $\checkmark$\\
\texttt{error = FALSE} & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\times$\\
\addlinespace
\texttt{include = FALSE} & $\checkmark$ & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}

}

\end{table}%

In addition to full chunks, you can embed small pieces of R code
directly within text using \emph{inline code}. This is done with
backticks and the \texttt{r} prefix. For example:

\begin{quote}
The factorial of 5 is
\texttt{\textasciigrave{}r\ factorial(5)\textasciigrave{}}.
\end{quote}

This renders as:

\begin{quote}
The factorial of 5 is 120.
\end{quote}

Inline code is useful when reporting values that should update
automatically when the document is rendered, such as sample sizes,
means, model results, or dates. This helps keep the written
interpretation consistent with the underlying analysis.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Practice:} Create a new R Markdown file and add a code chunk that
calculates the mean of a numeric vector. Then use inline code to display
that mean in a sentence.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Formatting Text}\label{formatting-text}

Clear, well-structured text is an essential part of any data report. In
R Markdown, ordinary text can be combined with simple Markdown syntax to
create headings, emphasize terms, organize lists, add links, and write
mathematical notation. These tools help make reports easier to read and
interpret.

Headings are created using one or more \texttt{\#} symbols. For example,
\texttt{\#} creates a main section, \texttt{\#\#} creates a subsection,
and \texttt{\#\#\#} creates a lower-level subsection. Emphasis can be
added using asterisks: italic text is written as \texttt{*italic*},
while bold text is written as \texttt{**bold**}.

Lists can be created by starting each item with \texttt{-} or
\texttt{*}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\SpecialStringTok{{-} }\NormalTok{First item}
\SpecialStringTok{{-} }\NormalTok{Second item}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Hyperlinks are written by placing the link text in square brackets and
the web address in parentheses. For example,
\texttt{{[}R\ Markdown\ website{]}(https://rmarkdown.rstudio.com)}
creates a clickable link to the R Markdown website.

R Markdown also supports mathematical notation using LaTeX-style syntax.
Inline equations are enclosed in single dollar signs, such as
\texttt{\$y\ =\ \textbackslash{}beta\_0\ +\ \textbackslash{}beta\_1\ x\$}.
Display equations are enclosed in double dollar signs and appear on a
separate line:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{$$}
\NormalTok{y = \textbackslash{}beta\_0 + \textbackslash{}beta\_1 x}
\NormalTok{$$}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Mathematical expressions render well in HTML and PDF output, although
support may vary across output formats. These basic formatting tools are
sufficient for the simple reports created in this chapter; more advanced
formatting options can be explored as needed.

\subsection*{Learning More About R
Markdown}\label{learning-more-about-r-markdown}

As readers gain experience with R, R Markdown can support increasingly
complete reproducible workflows. Beyond simple reports, it can be used
to document data preparation, exploratory analysis, modeling,
visualizations, and interpretation in a single source file. This helps
ensure that code, results, and written conclusions remain connected as
an analysis develops.

Readers who want to learn more may consult the \emph{R Markdown Cheat
Sheet} (Grolemund, n.d.), which provides a concise overview of common
syntax and options. A more detailed reference is \emph{R Markdown: The
Definitive Guide} (Xie et al. 2018), which covers document structure,
formatting, output formats, and more advanced uses of R Markdown.

A reproducible document can record work across the Data Science
Workflow, including Data Acquisition, Data Understanding and
Exploration, Data Preparation for Modeling, Modeling, and Model
Evaluation, while also documenting the decisions and results needed for
communication and Deployment. The aim at this stage is not to learn
every feature of R Markdown, but to become comfortable creating simple,
reproducible reports that combine code, output, and explanation.

\section{Chapter Summary and
Takeaways}\label{chapter-summary-and-takeaways-8}

This chapter introduced the practical R foundations needed to follow the
examples, case studies, and exercises throughout the book. We began by
setting up R and RStudio, distinguishing between working interactively
in the console and writing reusable code in scripts. We then introduced
R packages, including the distinction between installing a package once
and loading it in each new R session.

We also covered basic R code, objects, comments, functions, and common
operators. The chapter showed how data can be loaded from R packages or
imported from external files, and why reproducible analyses should make
data-loading steps explicit in code. We also discussed working
directories, RStudio Projects, and relative file paths as practical
tools for organizing analyses.

Finally, we introduced common data types and data structures, with
particular emphasis on data frames as the central structure for tabular
data. We used \textbf{ggplot2} to create simple visualizations, briefly
introduced formula notation used in the modeling chapters, and showed
how R Markdown can combine code, output, and explanation in a
reproducible report. Together, these foundations provide the R skills
needed to work with the Data Science Workflow introduced in Chapter
\ref{sec-chapter-intro-data-science} and applied throughout the book.

\section{Exercises}\label{sec-R-exercises}

The exercises below reinforce the practical R foundations introduced in
this chapter. They begin with conceptual questions, then move to basic R
practice, working with data, visualization, reporting, and reflection.

\subsection*{Conceptual Understanding}\label{conceptual-understanding-1}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Explain the difference between installing a package and loading a
  package in R. Why is \texttt{install.packages()} usually needed only
  once, while \texttt{library()} is needed in each new R session?
\item
  What is the difference between a data type and a data structure in R?
  Give one example of each.
\item
  Explain why using an RStudio Project and relative file paths is
  usually preferable to repeatedly using \texttt{setwd()} inside
  scripts.
\item
  In \textbf{ggplot2}, what is the difference between mapping an
  aesthetic inside \texttt{aes()} and setting an aesthetic outside
  \texttt{aes()}? Use color as an example.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Basic R Practice}\label{basic-r-practice}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{4}
\item
  Install R and RStudio on your computer, if they are not already
  installed. Open RStudio and run a simple calculation in the console,
  such as \texttt{2\ +\ 3}.
\item
  Create a numeric vector called \texttt{numbers} containing the values
  5, 10, 15, 20, and 25. Compute its mean and standard deviation.
\item
  Create a \(3 \times 4\) matrix containing the integers from 1 through
  12. Use \texttt{dim()} to check its dimensions and retrieve the value
  in the second row and third column.
\item
  Create a data frame with the columns \texttt{student\_id},
  \texttt{name}, \texttt{score}, and \texttt{passed}. Populate it with
  at least five rows of sample data and inspect it using
  \texttt{head()}, \texttt{str()}, and \texttt{summary()}.
\item
  Define \texttt{x\ =\ 7} and \texttt{y\ =\ 5}. Compute
  \texttt{x\ +\ y}, \texttt{x\ \textgreater{}\ y}, and
  \texttt{(x\ \textgreater{}\ 1)\ \&\ (y\ \textless{}\ 5)}. Then change
  the values of \texttt{x} and \texttt{y} and evaluate the expressions
  again.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Working with Data}\label{working-with-data}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{9}
\item
  Install and load the \textbf{liver} package. Then load the
  \texttt{churn} dataset and inspect its structure using
  \texttt{str(churn)}.
\item
  Use \texttt{head()} to display the first rows of \texttt{churn}, and
  use \texttt{dim()} to report the number of observations and variables.
\item
  Use \texttt{summary()} to generate descriptive summaries for the
  variables in \texttt{churn}. Identify at least two numerical variables
  and one categorical variable.
\item
  Apply \texttt{class()} and \texttt{typeof()} to several columns of
  \texttt{churn}. Compare the results and explain what each function
  tells you.
\item
  Create a small example with two data frames that share an \texttt{id}
  column. Use \texttt{merge()} to perform an inner join and a left join.
  Compare the number of rows in the two results.
\item
  Use \texttt{getwd()} to check your current working directory. Then
  create or open an RStudio Project and consider how a file stored in a
  folder called \texttt{data} could be imported using a relative path
  such as \texttt{"data/my\_file.csv"}.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Visualization and
Reporting}\label{visualization-and-reporting}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{15}
\item
  Load the \textbf{ggplot2} package and create a scatter plot of
  \texttt{transaction\_amount\_12} versus
  \texttt{transaction\_count\_12} using the \texttt{churn} dataset.
\item
  Create a histogram of \texttt{transaction\_amount\_12} using
  \texttt{geom\_histogram()}. What does the plot show about the
  distribution of this variable?
\item
  Create a boxplot of \texttt{transaction\_amount\_12}, grouped by
  \texttt{churn} status. What does the plot suggest about differences
  between the two groups?
\item
  Create two scatter plots of \texttt{transaction\_amount\_12} versus
  \texttt{transaction\_count\_12}. In the first plot, map color to the
  \texttt{churn} variable inside \texttt{aes()}. In the second plot, set
  a fixed color outside \texttt{aes()}. Compare the interpretation of
  the two plots.
\item
  Create a simple R Markdown report that includes a title, your name,
  one code chunk that loads or explores the \texttt{churn} dataset, and
  one visualization. Render the report to HTML.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Extension Exercises}\label{extension-exercises}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
